### On the
## *Reverend and Most Excellent*
## *Man*
# Lord THEODORIC Hackspan, <note>Theodoric (Dietrich) Hackspan (1607–1659) was a noted Lutheran theologian and Orientalist at the University of Altdorf.</note>
### MOST RENOWNED THEOLOGIAN AND PHILOSOPHER,
### DEATH.

Those whom an equality of studies had joined for many years;
These a single day of sad fate separates.
Heavenly rest is won for you, HACKSPAN! your body
The earth covers: your fame flies through the mouths of men. <note>original: "volitat fama per ora virum" — a phrase famously used by the Roman poet Virgil, suggesting that the deceased’s reputation will live on through the speech of the living.</note>
But the anxiety of my labors exhausts me:
Hence I long for the quiet dwellings of my Father's heaven.
One day shall join us again in the citadel above.
O, may that day come more swiftly to us!

->Pastor and Public Professor<-
->in Nuremberg.<-

Both **Duty toward the deceased** and **Charity toward our neighbor** demand that the writings and scholarly labors <note>The original Latin "lucubrationes" refers specifically to work produced by lamplight, implying late-night, diligent study.</note> of learned men should not be suppressed, but rather be released to the public. **Duty toward the deceased** requires that those things which have been discovered and thought out with great effort by erudite men should come forth under the names of their own authors. This is done so that the deserved praise—which is almost the only reward for literature—might return to the true authors, and also so that the opportunity might be snatched away from those who **adorn themselves with borrowed feathers** <note>original Greek: "ἀλλοτρίοις πτερõις καλλωπίζονται" — an allusion to Aesop’s fables, where a bird dresses in the feathers of others to appear more beautiful.</note>, preventing them from pouncing on the **unpublished** <note>original Greek: "ἀνέκδοτα" (anekdota), meaning literally "not given out" or "not published."</note> writings of others and stealing the **bread kneaded by others** <note>original Greek: "μάζαν ὑφ' ἑτέρων μεμαγμένην" — a proverbial expression for taking credit for someone else's hard work.</note>. **Charity toward our neighbor** demands the same thing. ### OF THE FIRST BOOK
# OF THE MISCELLANIES
### CHAPTER ONE.
#### CONCERNING
## THE SYNECDOCHE OF A PART
## FOR A PART.

->§. I.<-

Rhetorical handbooks commonly present a twofold Synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole, or the whole for a part; for example, referring to a car as "wheels."</note>; *one* in which a part is put for the whole, and *the other* in which the whole is put for a part. Those who debated controversies in the age and memory of our ancestors, by no means content with that number, added a *third* species, in which one part takes the place of another part. The reasons for initiating this dispute are primarily twofold: the *first* is that, since in *Psalm 16, 10* we read "You will not abandon my soul to the grave" <note>original Hebrew: לא־תעזב נפשׁי לשׁאול (*lo-ta'azov nafshi lish'ol*)</note>, the followers of Calvin—be they his "sons" or his "grandsons" <note>Likely referring to the second or third generation of Reformed theologians who followed John Calvin’s teachings.</note> as they are called—interpret *Sheol* <note>original: שׁאול (*she'ol*); the Hebrew realm of the dead, often translated as the grave or hell.</note> as the Grave, and *Nephesh* <note>original: נפשׁ (*nephesh*); soul or life force.</note> [as life or body]...

<meta>The text breaks off here at the end of the page; the catchword "de" (of) indicates the sentence continues on the next page, likely defining "Nephesh" as a part of the person standing in for another part.</meta>

### FIRST BOOK OF MISCELLANIES

...as a body prepared for burial—that is, a corpse—doubting not that this is the true version of the passage: *you will not leave my corpse in the tomb.* <note>original Latin: "non relinques Cadaver meum in sepulcro." This refers to a controversial interpretation of Psalm 16:10, where "soul" (nephesh) is translated as "corpse" to avoid the implication of the soul staying in the grave.</note> One may consult <margin>(a) Book 2 of the Miscellanies, chapter 2.</margin> Theodore Beza <note>A major French Protestant theologian (1519–1605) and successor to John Calvin.</note> and Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish scholar and expert in Biblical languages.</note> on this. The second reason concerns the meaning of the words in Genesis 46:26: *All the souls coming with Jacob into Egypt, who issued from his thigh, were sixty-six* <note>original Hebrew: כָּל־הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַבָּאָה לְיַעֲקֹב מִצְרַיְמָה יֹצְאֵי יְרֵכֹוֹ שִׁשִּׁים וָשֵׁשׁ (*kol ha-nefesh ha-ba'ah le-Ya'akov Mitzraymah yotzei yerecho shishim va-shesh*)</note>. These words seemed to imply "Traducianism" <note>The doctrine that the human soul is transmitted through natural generation (parents) along with the body.</note> since there is an explicit mention of "souls" [being born]; but to avoid admitting this sense, the defenders of Creationism <note>The doctrine that God creates a new soul for every human body at the moment of conception.</note> interpreted "soul" as referring to the "body." They did this by a device that some find ridiculous: namely, that specific <term>Synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole, or here, one part represents another related part.</note>—previously unheard of and even considered improper—by which one part is substituted for another part.

But truly, whatever may be the case regarding the controversy itself—which is twofold, concerning the descent into hell and the origin of the rational soul, and which the chairs of both theologians and philosophers claim for themselves—I shall clearly show my own view on that Synecdoche, which pertains to *Rhetoric, a significant part of Sacred Philology* <note>The study of biblical texts through their original languages and literary structures.</note>. I will do this by first plainly presenting the arguments of my opponents, with all due respect to those who hold different views.

He announces his intention to analyze this linguistic phenomenon from the perspective of Sacred Philology.</summary>

II. Therefore, Bellarmine’s <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit Cardinal and Counter-Reformation theologian.</note> position is negative: "Usage," he says, "permits <term>Synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole (e.g., "all hands on deck" for "all sailors"), or the whole represents a part.</note>, through which we put a part for the whole and the reverse; however, it does not permit putting one part for another part." Likewise, Dr. T. T. says: "If he understands such a Synecdoche—one where an essential part is taken to mean another essential part that is distinctly different from it—he is mistaken. First, Rhetorically: let him produce a rule from the entire system of Rhetoric that contains such a Synecdoche, and he alone shall have Phyllis. <note>original Latin: "Phyllida solus habebit." A reference to Virgil’s Eclogues, meaning he would win the ultimate prize for doing the impossible.</note> Second, Theologically: let him unroll the entire Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>, run through the Major and Minor Prophets, and even the New Testament if he likes; he will never find a single example of his fictional Synecdoche." Master Dr. S. states: "A Synecdoche of a part for an opposing part does not exist." More recently, Master Dr. D. also says: "We decisively <note>original Greek: ἀποτόμως (*apotomos*), meaning 'sharply' or 'curtly.'</note> deny that any trope of Synecdoche exists that puts one part for another, using that very master of speech, USAGE, as our witness. For let them allege any approved author who uses a part for another part synecdochically, and they shall win the day."

<margin>
*Letter 157 to Optatus.*
</margin>
III. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose views on the soul's origin were central to these debates.</note> asserts that a part can be put for another part, but somewhat timidly; and so, lest he should clash with the rules of the Rhetoricians, he maintains that this happens in a mode of speaking by which that which is contained signifies that which contains. Regarding this opinion, I shall offer my own judgment below.

The author cites prominent theologians and the rules of rhetoric to argue that while a part can represent a whole, one part cannot represent a different, distinct part.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding synecdoche. # BOOK I. MISCELLANIES
<meta>catchword: bimus</meta>

<margin>Book 2 of the Miscellanies, chapter 8.</margin>
<margin>In the Treatise on the Creation of the Soul, page 115.</margin>
But *Johannes Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616) was a prominent Flemish Protestant scholar and Hebraist.</note> boldly opposes *Bellarmine*, confirming the affirmative position; *Schindler* follows him throughout his Lexicon, especially under the word <note>original Hebrew: נפש (nephesh), meaning soul, breath, or being.</note> *soul*, as does *Wagnereck*. I side with *Drusius* and *Schindler*, and before I address the objections to their examples, I will add others I have observed myself.

IV. To begin with, they [the opponents] demand an approved Author who might put one part for another, as they are persuaded that common usage speaks against this assertion. Truly, I have no intention of scouring every monument of the finest writers, especially since this dispute arose from Scripture, and the adversaries themselves have appealed to it.

<margin>Commentary on Book 14, chapter 4 of Augustine’s *City of God*.</margin>
Yet let a single example suffice, which *Nonius Marcellus* <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian and lexicographer.</note> cites in *Juan Luis Vives’* commentary from *Virgil*, and it is clear enough. For thus he [Virgil] says in Book II of the *Aeneid*:

> Meanwhile, let us commit our comrades and their unburied **BODIES** <note>original Latin: CORPORA</note> to the earth,
> Which is the only honor in the depths of the Acheron:
> Go, he said, grace with final gifts those illustrious **SOULS**, <note>original Latin: ANIMAS</note>
> Who won this fatherland for us with their own blood — — —

He would be blind who does not see that **SOULS** and **BODIES** are here exchanged for one another by a certain <term>Synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part is used for the whole or vice versa; here, the author argues "soul" is used to mean the physical corpse and "body" for the person.</note>.

V. If we indeed run through the Scriptures, we shall see manifest examples of this synecdoche everywhere.

<summary>The author argues against Bellarmine, claiming that "soul" and "body" can indeed be used interchangeably in literature and scripture. He cites Johannes Drusius and a specific passage from Virgil’s Aeneid to prove that classical and sacred texts use this rhetorical figure.</summary>

<keywords>Johannes Drusius, Robert Bellarmine, Valentin Schindler, Virgil, Aeneid, synecdoche, soul and body, linguistics, biblical philology</keywords>

# CHAPTER I OF THE MISCELLANIES
<meta>The header "NEORUM CAP. I." completes the word "MISCELLANEORUM" from the previous page's title.</meta>

... we will provide examples. Consider how **Luther**, who was as skilled as anyone in explaining the Scriptures and clarifying their phrasing, translates these words! 
<margin>Psalm 105:18.</margin>
In the original source <note>original Hebrew: ברזל באה נפשו (*barzel ba’ah naphsho*)</note> it reads: *Iron entered his soul*. Luther translated it: *His body had to lie in iron*. This is excellent. For according to **Abenezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a distinguished Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note>, there is an ellipsis <gloss>of the letter 'B'</gloss> in the <gloss>commentary</gloss> on the word <gloss>iron</gloss>; thus, "his soul <gloss>in this place</gloss> entered into iron." **Symmachus**, a Greek interpreter, says: *into iron* <note>original Greek: εἰς σίδηρον</note>. Compare also the **Syriac** and **Arabic** versions. However, the **Chaldean** <note>The Targum, or Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> explains this through a *hypallage* <note>A figure of speech where the natural relations of two words are reversed.</note> in this manner: *A chain of iron was applied to his soul* <note>original Aramaic: שיד דפרזל עלת בנפשיה</note>, which also occurs in Judges 1:8: *they sent the city into the fire*, instead of: *they sent fire into the city*. **Pellicanus** in his commentary on this passage, **Schindler** in his Lexicon, **Vatablus** in his Notes, **Drusius**, and **Buxtorf** in his Lexicon under the word *iron* <note>original Hebrew: ברזל (*barzel*)</note> all side with Luther. 
<margin>Book 2 of the Miscellanies, chapter 13.</margin>
These are men famous in every quarter, born to cultivate these letters.

6. Do you demand Greek examples? Indeed, they provide these: 
<margin>Genesis 36:6.</margin>
Esau took *all the souls of his house* <note>original Hebrew: את-כל-נפשות ביתו (*et-kol-naphshot beito*)</note>. The Greeks rendered this: *all the bodies of his house* <note>original Greek: πάντα τὰ σώματα τοῦ οἴκου αὐτοῦ</note>. And 
<margin>Isaiah 58:5.</margin>
*have I chosen this fast, that a man should bow down* **his head**? <note>original Hebrew: ראשו (*rosho*)</note>. The Greeks translated this as: **the neck** <note>original Greek: τὸν τραχήλου</note>. Here, clearly, the neck is used in place of the head.

unnecessary, or spurious; according to **Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a leading Renaissance scholar of linguistics and logic</note>, they are introduced either due to a lack of other words, the invention of new things, to provide elegance to speech, or finally, due to a lazy ignorance of philology. The reasoning for this is sought from the nature of words, which are signs representing things and manifesting concepts; indeed, they are even like images displaying the appearance of a thing. But an image does not display a thing, except for one; it relates to others only by accident. For an Ethiopian does not resemble Absalom, nor does a raven resemble a swan. If a word sounded out opposites equally and primarily, how would it perform its duty? How would it manifest a concept? 16. If I wish to know, in this present case, which meaning of a word is ultimately the primary and proper one, know that it can be investigated in three ways:

I. From the origin; namely, when either a noun descends from a verb as from something simpler—for example, *malkut* <note>Hebrew: מַלְכוּת, meaning "kingdom"</note> from *malak* <note>Hebrew: מָלַךְ, meaning "he reigned"</note>, "kingdom" from "he reigned"—or a verb from a noun, such as *he’ezin* <note>Hebrew: הֶאֱזִין, meaning "he listened"</note> from *ozen* <note>Hebrew: אֹזֶן, meaning "ear"</note>, "he heard" from "ear." Just as a son, by way of his form, represents his parents as univocal causes <term>univocal causes: in traditional logic, a cause that produces an effect of the exact same nature as itself</term>, so too a word, by way of its meaning, reflects the origin or root from which it sprouts. For the meaning is the "form" of a word <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "form" is the essential nature or defining characteristic of a thing</note>. This is a point that the Papists <note>original: "Pontificii"; referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> are so far from denying that they frequently cry out that Protestants are deprived of the true Bible...

III. Moreover, these indicators or arguments must be joined together; and what cannot be proven by each individually should be proven by all of them together as a whole.

17. Now, all these proofs <note>original Greek: πείσματα (peismata) — persuasive arguments or proofs</note> demonstrate that *nefesh* <note>Hebrew: נפש</note> properly signifies "soul"; however, all evidence stands in the way of it likewise properly signifying "body." 

I. Whether you establish *nefesh* as a primitive word <term>primitive: a root word not derived from any other</term> from which verbs descend, or as a derivative descending from the root *n-f-sh* (which is not in use today), the conclusion remains sound. For among the Hebrews, the verb form of *nefesh* means "he breathed," or "he recovered his spirit or hope," which refers to the soul as the cause of life and respiration. Among the Syrians <note>referring to the Syriac language</note> and the Rabbinic Chaldeans <note>Aramaic</note>, the word means "he animated" or "he restored the spirit," and in Arabic it means to be of a tranquil mind or to take heart.

II. As for the usage of authors—and indeed their most frequent usage—I could prove it to no one who is ignorant of these letters <note>meaning the Hebrew alphabet and language</note>; yet no one who is even moderately skilled in them would deny it.

III. The consensus and harmony of languages is clear. For what is called *nefesh* by the Hebrews is *nafsha* <note>original Chaldean: נַפְשָׁא</note> to the Chaldean; *nafsha* <note>original Syriac: ܢܰܦܫܳܐ</note> to the Syrian; and *nafs* <note>original Arabic: نَفْس</note> to the Arab.

# BOOK I. MISCELLANY — and the soul [is laid] in the tomb

<warning>Large water stain on the left margin; text remains legible.</warning>

-> — — *and the soul in the tomb* <-
-> *We lay* — <-
<note>original Latin: *animamque sepulcro condimus*. A quotation from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book 3, line 68, describing a funeral rite. The author uses this classical reference to show that even in Latin, the "soul" is poetically said to be placed in a grave.</note>

This passage is to be compared with the other one proposed in section 4.

18. Nor are the arguments of Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621) was a highly influential Jesuit Cardinal and a central figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note> of any weight. To his first point, I respond: 1. Grammar does not admit these kinds of dialectical <term>dialectical: relating to logical argumentation or the investigation of truth through discussion</term> reasonings. For words are chosen by convention <note>original Latin: *ad placitum* — by choice or whim</note> and depend upon the usage of speakers, as the Cardinal himself says in the cited passage. II. It follows only that "soul" is not properly used to describe a corpse <note>original Latin: *cadaver*</note>, in which there is a deprivation of life. Indeed, no one asserts this except perhaps Bellarmine, who says that *nefesh* <note>Hebrew: נֶפֶשׁ</note> properly signifies something indifferent to both the living and the non-living. Rather, it is a synecdoche <term>synecdoche: a figure of speech where a part represents the whole (e.g., "wheels" for a car)</term> of a part for a part, when *nefesh* is used to mean "corpse"; and it is such a synecdoche that it is joined with catachresis. For catachresis <term>catachresis: the use of a word in a way that departs from its literal or traditional meaning, often a strained or forced metaphor</term> is not a unique figure of speech <term>tropus: a figurative use of an expression</term>, but a common quality spread and diffused through all species of figures. Thus, we encounter harsher metaphors and metonymies, as well as synecdochic and ironic expressions. 

Antiphrasis <term>antiphrasis: the use of a word in a sense opposite to its proper meaning</term> is also not unusual in Hebrew. For example: 
* *Berakh* <note>Hebrew: בֵּרַךְ</note> can mean both "to bless" and "to curse." 
* *Sakhal* <note>Hebrew: סָכַל</note> can mean "constancy" and "inconstancy." 
* *Chesed* <note>Hebrew: חֶסֶד</note> can mean "mercy" and "cruelty" or "reproach." 
* *Ervah* <note>Hebrew: עֶרְוָה</note> signifies "nakedness" or a thing that should by no means be uncovered.

<summary>The author rejects Cardinal Bellarmine's claim that the Hebrew word for "soul" (nefesh) can literally mean "body," arguing instead that such instances are figures of speech like synecdoche or antiphrasis. He explains that in many languages, including Hebrew and Latin, words are often used to mean their opposites or related concepts through poetic license rather than strict definition.</summary>

To the second point, I respond that it does not follow: *nefesh* <note>Hebrew: נֶפֶשׁ — soul or breath</note> signifies something indifferent to the living and the non-living; therefore it is so because the word *chayah* <note>Hebrew: חַיָּה — living</note> is added. Compare this with the passage cited from **1 Corinthians**.

III. Even if the text were read exactly as the Vulgate has it, **Bellarmine** <note>Cardinal Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a major Catholic theologian whom the author is refuting.</note> would still prove nothing. For even with [grammatical] suffixes, the word refers to the **subject** <term>the individual person or "self"</term>. Thus *min-nafsho* <note>Hebrew: מִנַּפְשׂוֹ</note> is "from himself," and *min-nafshecha* <note>Hebrew: מִנַּפְשְׁךָ</note> is "from yourself." So much for Bellarmine’s exception.

<meta>This page continues the philological argument regarding the term "soul" (nefesh/psyche). It completes the word "Hellenism" from the previous page and argues that "soul" and "body" are not interchangeable general categories, but specific terms that only refer to one another through figurative speech.</meta>

<page-num>4.</page-num>
<header>BOOK I. MISCELLA-</header>

[Helle]nism, they contend that these are general terms with respect to the soul and the body, and are thus indifferent to whether something is living or non-living. They argue that if these terms are taken to represent the body, it is a **synecdoche** <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole, or a general category represents a specific one.</note> of the genus <note>The general category.</note> for the species <note>The specific type.</note>. 

In truth, however, such a synecdoche only holds if one word truly functions as a genus and the other as a species. This occurs when "mortals" or *creatures* <note>original: בריות (*beriyot*)</note> in **Mark 16:16** <note>The author likely refers to Mark 16:15: "Preach the gospel to every creature."</note> are used to mean "men"; or if the word "bird" is used for a "hen," or "animal" for a "beast," or "star" is understood specifically as "the Dog-star" or "Sirius." In these cases, a species is considered to stand for a genus when it truly is a member of that category. 

But where a single word signifies one thing properly and another thing improperly <note>That is, figuratively or metaphorically.</note>, then the relationship of genus and species does not apply. Consequently, it is neither a synecdoche of genus for species, nor the reverse. 

Now, just as the word *soul* <note>original: נפש (*nefesh*)</note> has only one proper and primary meaning, so too does the Greek word *soul* <note>original: ψυχὴ (*psyche*)</note>. Even if it is used in the Hellenistic <note>The Greek style used by Jewish scholars and New Testament writers.</note> sense, it properly signifies the "soul"—the other part of a human being—and only by synecdoche does it signify the "body" or "corpse." It cannot be a genus <note>A general category including both body and soul.</note> because of its improper <note>figurative</note> usage. 

Thus, whatever word allows for a figurative interpretation alongside its proper one, if you accept it in one specific way, it will be a synecdoche of genus for species—even if it were used properly in the text. For example, the word "soul" <note>original: *anima*</note> when it is used to mean the "body" in the works of the **Psalmist** <note>The author of the biblical Psalms.</note> and **Virgil** <note>The Roman poet; the author is comparing biblical language to classical Latin literature.</note>, or for the soul in other [passages]...

24. IV. Others, even if they grant that one part can be substituted for another part, nevertheless deny that this is a **synecdoche** <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole (like "hired hands" for "workers").</note>. Instead, they refer it to a **metonymy** <note>A figure of speech where an object is called by the name of something associated with it (like "the Crown" for "the King").</note> of the "contained for the container," as we mentioned in section 3 above regarding **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential philosopher and theologian.</note>, and as is evident from **Amesius** <note>William Ames (1576–1633), an English Protestant theologian.</note> in his response to the previously cited passage by **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and major figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note>. **Wagnereckius** <note>Heinrich Wagnereck (1614–1667), a Jesuit theologian known for his works on law and logic.</note> responds that substituting the "contained for the container" does indeed belong to the category of synecdoche. For my part, while I would not grant that just any metonymy can be called a synecdoche by the rhetoricians—since there exists a relationship of container and contained where neither is strictly a "part" of the other—I am moved by the fact that it should be called a "part-for-a-part synecdoche" rather than metonymy. This is because in sections 6 and 7, examples are read which do not involve the relationship of container and contained at all; therefore, it is more of an incidental feature of a synecdoche if a relationship of container and contained happens to be present. Nevertheless, this is a dispute over a name.

25. This is my opinion on the **Synecdoche**, which has been so often insisted upon. Even the **logicians** up to now have treated universal statements that are affirmative in appearance, but in sense...

...it is so. Nor is the reasoning of **Scultetus** of such great weight, which he draws from the connection or the particle *for* <note>original Greek: γὰρ (*gar*)</note> that **Matthew** adds. In this way, indeed, if actual usage is set aside, the rules of **Grammar** are applied incorrectly. For frequently, what holds true when speaking in absolute terms cannot be rightly used in comparison or in relation to a specific phrase. Therefore, whatever comes of this reconciliation, **Scultetus** certainly did not "hit the nail on the head," as they say.

We admit that this is sometimes the case, but here they coincide, just as elsewhere the word *yatsa* <note>original Hebrew: יָצָא, meaning to go out or come forth</note> is applied to birth, as in **Genesis 35:11**, *and kings shall come forth from your loins* <note>original Hebrew: וּמְלָכִים מֵחֲלָצֶיךָ יֵצֵאוּ</note>. In **Judges 8:30**, <note>The text cites Chapter 9, but the reference to Gideon's seventy sons is in 8:30</note> **Gideon** had seventy sons *who came out of his thigh* <note>original Hebrew: יֹצְאֵי יְרֵכוֹ; a Hebrew idiom for biological descendants</note>. In **Job 1:21**, <note>The text cites 1:25</note> *naked I came forth from my mother’s womb* <note>original Hebrew: יָצָאתִי מִבֶּטֶן אִמִּי</note>. Sometimes it occurs alone, without other words added, as in **Genesis 10:14**, *from whom the Philistines came forth* <note>original Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר יָצְאוּ מִשָּׁם פְּלִשְׁתִּים</note>, and **1 Chronicles 2:53**, *from these were born* <note>original Hebrew: מֵאֵלֶּה יָצְאוּ</note>. The same applies here, where the discussion concerns a town, to which neither a "thigh," nor a "womb," nor "loins" are appropriate.

XIV. But what need is there for many words? By the term *motsa’ot* <note>original Hebrew: מוֹצָאוֹת, translated as "goings forth"</note> is understood either a local departure, or a family lineage, or finally, a divine generation.

Not those things; for besides the fact that the **Photinians** <note>Followers of the 4th-century bishop Photinus; in this period, the term was used to label Socinians or Unitarians who denied the pre-existence of Christ.</note> are not concerned with it, a dignity ought to be added to this "going forth" from the town of **Bethlehem**, such that it is far superior to all the most famous cities of **Judah**. Truly, a mere local going forth or physical movement does not provide this, though such movement is attributed to the **Messiah** (about whom all the **Jews** agree with the **Photinians**) even in respect to those other cities. *Not those either*, both because a family is never called "goings forth" <note>original Hebrew: מוצאות, *motsa’ot*</note> by the **Hebrews**, but rather *house* <note>original Hebrew: בית, *bayit*</note>, or *family* <note>original Hebrew: משפחה, *mishpachah*</note>, or *generations* <note>original Hebrew: תולדות, *toldot*</note>, or finally *tribes* <note>original Hebrew: שבטים, *shevatim*</note>; and **Christ** is called, by reason of family, the son or seed of **Abraham** or **David**, with the name of the head of the family added. Furthermore, the *goings forth* of the **Messiah** are attributed to him *from of old, from the days of eternity* <note>original Hebrew: מקדם מימי עולם, *mi-qedem mi-yemei olam*</note>; that family—namely the **Davidic** line, which the **Photinians** understand this to mean—did not extend itself back that far. And if he had wanted to commend **Christ** by way of a famous and ancient family, he could have instead traced his origin from **Abraham**, which would have been a far longer duration than the **Davidic** line.

XVI. However, neither the phrase *mi-qedem* <note>original Hebrew: מקדם, meaning "from of old" or "from the East"</note> nor the word *mi-yemei* <note>original Hebrew: מימי, meaning "from the days of"</note> prevents us from concluding that "eternity" in its proper sense is meant here. For *mi-qedem*, which is understood everywhere as referring to ancient days, is used neutrally for that which took its beginning in time, and for that which acknowledges no beginning of time. Therefore, it can be translated as: "from a former time," "from the beginning," or *before the beginning*—that is, before the world—which is elsewhere expressed as: *before the foundation of the world* <note>original Greek: πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου (*pro katabolēs kosmou*)</note>. Furthermore, the words *mi-yemei olam* <note>original Hebrew: מימי עולם, "from the days of eternity/antiquity"</note> specifically signify an eternity that one estimates from the beginning of the world; and that is the very description of the eternal **GOD**: that He was *olam* <note>eternity/everlasting</note> or *yom* <note>day</note> before the world existed, and before there was any day. Clearly, there is a gradation in the text...

Not even the philosophers themselves can avoid this; they deny that God occupies a "place," yet they use adverbs of place when they argue about what is *above the Heavens*.

V. Thus he argues: but he has not grasped the meaning of Moses <note>The traditional author of the Book of Deuteronomy, from which the verse in question is taken.</note>. For the word *chalaq* among the Hebrews is not used in the *Kal* <note>The "Kal" is the most basic, simple form of a verb in Hebrew grammar.</note> except in "two ways" <note>original Hebrew: שׁני פנים (*shenei panim*)</note> — that is, in a dual sense. First, in the "sense of division" <note>original Hebrew: לשׁון חלוק (*leshon chaluq*)</note>; then, second, in the "sense of softness and smoothness" <note>original Hebrew: לשׁון חלקות (*leshon chalaqot*)</note>. But in the *Hiphil* <note>The "Hiphil" is a causative verb form in Hebrew, often changing the meaning of the root.</note>, the word *hechliq* <note>original: החליק</note> is properly "to soften" or "to smooth," and figuratively, "to flatter." Therefore, whoever understands Moses as speaking of "flattery" confuses the literal meaning with the figurative, and fails to observe the distinction between the *Kal* and *Hiphil* verb forms—a distinction that is of the utmost necessity to observe.

It might indeed seem that a passage from **Psalm 55:22** favors that opinion: "the buttered words of his mouth were smooth" <note>original: חלקו מחמאות פיו (*chalaqu machma'ot piv*)</note>, in which words flattery is noted. However, that flattery is not suggested by the word *chalaqu* <note>original: חלקו</note> alone, but by the entire phrase. This is just as the expression "to untie the laces of one’s shoes" is used to indicate an act of service; the meaning is found in the whole idiom, not in the word "untie" by itself. Furthermore, if the discussion here were about "flattery" or "enticement," the Jews would possess nothing unique to themselves in this regard; for this to them...

VI. The **Jews** record that this passage is among those fourteen Sayings which the **Seventy Interpreters** <term>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally said to have been translated by 72 scholars; often abbreviated as "LXX."</term> altered while transferring the Hebrew speech into Greek. These are listed **in the book** *Yalkut* <note>The *Yalkut Shimoni*, a medieval compilation of Jewish midrashic (interpretive) traditions.</note> **at Genesis 1:1**. Seventy-two interpreters were assigned to as many individual cells so that they were separated from one another; nevertheless, they produced not a different version, but exactly the same Greek translation. It is said, however, that they did not change the text itself, but rather adapted the translation to suit the text. For example, at **Genesis 1:1**, they changed the order in this way: *God created in the beginning* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים ברא בראשית (*Elohim bara bereshit*)</note>; this was done so that God Himself would not be said to have been created by some unknown "Beginning" <note>The original Hebrew word order "Bereshit bara Elohim" could be misinterpreted by a Greek speaker as "In-the-beginning [a subject] created God."</note>. XI. Finally, the view of **Sixtinus Amama** <note>A Dutch Hebraist and professor of Hebrew (1593–1629).</note> in his *Critique on this passage* does not please me either. He understands that word *portion* <note>original Hebrew: חלק (*cheleq*), meaning a portion, territory, or inheritance.</note> as referring to that division by which specific stars were assigned to specific regions, such that there are many stars which, in our hemisphere, either never show themselves at all, or only appear through the changes of months and years. For, firstly, the Sun is also mentioned in the text, which is common to the Jews as well as the Gentiles every year and every day. Secondly, it is said that *God* has *apportioned* <note>original: *chalaq*</note> these to all peoples under the whole heaven. It is better, therefore, that we explain the word *portion* not as the act of divine division itself, but as a **permission**. This means that while the nations—by the permission of the Divine Power <note>original: *Numine*</note> according to His just judgment—wandered in the object of their worship, they adopted for themselves some stars as gods or lesser deities <note>original: *deastros*</note>. Necessity compels me to stoop to this interpretation; I am urged by the explanation of the Scriptures in **Acts 14:16**, where it is expressly said: *In past generations God permitted* <note>original Greek: εἴασε (*eiase*), meaning to allow or let be.</note> *all nations to go their own ways, although he did not leave himself without witness, giving rains from heaven.* Compare a similar point regarding the Jews in **Psalm 81:12-13** <note>In many Latin Bibles, this is cited as Psalm 81; in English Bibles, it corresponds to Psalm 81:11-12, "So I gave them up to their own hearts' lust."</note>.

XI. Finally, the view of **Sixtinus Amama** <note>A Dutch Hebraist and theologian (1593–1629) known for his work on the Hebrew text of the Bible.</note> in his *Censure on this passage* is also unsatisfactory. He interprets that word **portion** <note>original Hebrew: חלק (*helek*), meaning a share, territory, or allotment.</note> as referring to that astronomical division by which specific stars are assigned to specific regions, so that there are many stars which never show themselves at all in our hemisphere, or only appear through the changes of months and years. However, in the first place, the text also speaks of the Sun, which is common to both the Jews and the Gentiles every year and every day. Secondly, it is said that *God* **allotted** <note>original Hebrew: חלק (*helek*)</note> *them to all peoples under the whole heaven.* It is better, therefore, that we explain the word **allotted** not as the physical act of divine division, but as a "permission." That is to say, while the nations—the Divine Power permitting it out of a just judgment—adopted for themselves various stars as gods (or beings derived from stars), they wandered in the objective of their worship. Necessity compels me to go this far; I am urged by the explanation of the scriptures in **Acts 14:16**, where it is expressly said: *In past generations, God* **permitted** <note>original Greek: εἴασε (*eiase*)</note> *or let go all the nations to walk in their own ways, although he did not leave himself without witness, giving rains from heaven.* Compare a similar sentiment regarding the Jews in **Psalm 81:12-13** <note>"So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices."</note>.

Having considered this, I will complete the entire treatment in three sections. The first will recount various interpretations. The second will search for the genuine sense; the last will offer a most free judgment regarding the consequences and interpretations brought forward in the first section. For freedom, according to **Cunaeus** <note>Petrus Cunaeus (1586–1638), a Dutch scholar famous for his work on the Hebrew state.</note>, *is the soul of judgment, especially in Philology <note>The study of ancient texts and languages to understand their meaning.</note>, where, as long as one’s faith remains intact, one is permitted to depart into all other opinions.* For certainly, we who are devoted to sacred Philology are not **honey-cakes** <note>original: *placentae*. A Latin pun on the verb *placere* (to please). The author means they are not "sweet" things meant to please everyone.</note>, so that we might be able to please everyone, nor indeed should we be, since not everyone pleases us, and in our own court we are the judges—as **Drusius** <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a renowned Flemish Protestant scholar of the Bible and Hebrew.</note> wittily jokes. We are far from wishing to be considered the **parrots** of others, who repeat words and sounds without thinking, and blather out things sometimes correctly and sometimes perversely, as if someone else were speaking. He was a very great man indeed. 

To be sure, we follow **Luther**, who in his *Treatise on the Enslaved Will* <note>original: *De servo arbitrio*, Martin Luther's 1525 work arguing against free will in the context of salvation.</note> pays no heed to **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible, often seen as the ultimate authority in the Middle Ages.</note> when he disapproves. For he says: *We do not dispute about the meaning of Jerome, but about the meaning of Scripture; I do not allow myself to be pulled away from the greater authority by a lesser one, nor is Jerome so great that I should desert Paul <note>The Apostle Paul, whose writings are central to Luther’s theology.</note> for his sake. For we are not slaves, that we should fear to dissent from him in the explanation of any passage.*

...so that we may know the words themselves. III. **Blessed Luther** translated it: *Is it not thus: if you are pious, then you are acceptable?* From this, the **Remonstrants** <note>A group of Dutch Protestants (Arminians) who broke with strict Calvinism over the issue of free will and predestination.</note> weave such a version: *is it not so, if you do well, there will be acceptance or you will be accepted, etc. (Confession, Section 4).* Furthermore, in their *Apology for the Confession*, they conclude that *God loves and holds as pleasing internal actions that are morally good in themselves more than bare persons. For they say: It is not because the person is pleasing for whatever reason that such actions please; but on the contrary, because those actions please, the person is pleasing.*

<header>### BOOK I. MISCELLANIES</header>

In my consideration of this matter, I shall complete the entire treatment in three sections. The **first** will relate various interpretations. The **second** will search for the genuine sense; and the **final** section will offer a very free judgment concerning the consequences and interpretations brought forward in the first section. For freedom, as **Cunaeus** <note>Petrus Cunaeus (1586–1638), a Dutch scholar famous for his work on the Hebrew Republic.</note> asserts, *belongs to the soul of judgment, especially in <term>Philology</term> <note>The study of language in historical and literary texts.</note>, where, as long as the faith is kept safe, one is permitted to depart into all other opinions.* 

Certainly, we who are devoted to *sacred Philology* are not *the smoke of a cake* <note>original: "placentæ non fumus". This is a Latin idiom referring to a "crowd-pleaser" or someone who offers empty flattery to gain favor.</note> so that we might please everyone; nor indeed should we be, since not everyone pleases us, and in our own court we are the judges, as **Drusius** <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a celebrated Flemish Protestant biblical scholar and linguist.</note> playfully remarks. Far be it from us that we should wish to be considered *the parrots of others, who repeat words and sounds without a mind, and blather things now rightly, now wrongly spoken, as if someone else were speaking.* 

He was a man by far the greatest. Doubtless we follow **Luther**, who in his *Treatise on the Bondage of the Will* <note>original: "Tract. de servo arbitrio", Luther’s 1525 work arguing against Erasmus on the nature of human will and grace.</note> cares nothing for **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> when he approves too little of the text. *For,* [Luther] says, *we are not disputing about the sense of Jerome, but about the sense of Scripture: I do not allow myself to be torn from the greater authority by a lesser one, nor is Jerome so great that I should desert Paul for him.* <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> *For we are not slaves, that we should fear to disagree with someone in the explanation of a particular passage.*

III. **Blessed Luther** translated it as: *Is it not so? ...that man is endowed with free choice, he solemnly asserts, using these present words for that purpose. V. The **Latin Fathers** <note>The early Christian theologians of the Western Church who wrote in Latin.</note> presented such a version, following the **Greeks** <note>Referring to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>: *If you offer correctly, but do not divide correctly, have you not sinned? They argue that Cain, though offering correctly, divided the portions most poorly, having offered the baser things with no selection made. Therefore, after that sin was admitted, he, suffused with shame, is called to repentance. The Mainz Jesuit, **Johann Busæus** <note>Johannes Busæus (1547–1611), a Dutch Jesuit theologian.</note>, emphasizes this sense and this sequence from **Ambrose**, **Augustine**, and **Chrysostom** in his *Greenery of Christian Virtues, in the section on Offering oneself to God.*

VIII. The first rule is that of **Rabbi David Kimchi** in the *Michlol* <note>The *Michlol* is a foundational work on Hebrew grammar written by David Kimchi (c. 1160–1235), a celebrated rabbi and grammarian from Provence.</note>: *Because the infinitive is related to the noun, and the noun [derives] from the infinitive in the manner of a noun, so also the noun may be used in the sense of an infinitive* <note>original Hebrew: לפי שהמקור קרובים והשם ממקור בדרך השם וכן השם יבא בענין המקור</note>; that is, because a certain affinity exists between the infinitive and the noun, the infinitive is used for the noun and conversely the noun is used for the infinitive. For example, **Psalm 101:3**, *I have hated the doing of transgressions* <note>original Hebrew: עשות-סטים, using an infinitive</note>, that is, *the work or deed of transgressors* <note>original Hebrew: מעשה סטים, using a noun</note>. Add the passages **1 Samuel 15:12**, **Deuteronomy 25:2**, **Psalm 139:2**, **Isaiah 37:28**. However, examples of a noun being used in place of an infinitive are these: **Numbers 10:2**, **Deuteronomy 10:11**, where *le-masa* <note>original: למסע; literally "for the journey," a noun</note> is put for *le-hasa* <note>original: להסע; "to cause to journey," an infinitive</note>, meaning "to set out"; and in the **same chapter, verse 15**, *le-ahavah* <note>original: לאהבה; "for love," a noun</note> for *le-ahov* <note>original: לאהוב; "to love," an infinitive</note>. Compare **Esther 9:19** and **Ezekiel 17:9**.

IX. The **second rule** is this: not infrequently, something must be repeated from the preceding words *apo koinou* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ κοινῶ; a rhetorical device where a word is shared by two clauses or phrases</note>, and conversely, a word must be recalled from the following to the preceding, so that the sense may be clear. The first part of the rule is supported by many examples, where not only must a negative particle be repeated—which the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum, a translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> along with the Greek <note>The Septuagint.</note> also repeated in **Psalm 9:19**—but even nouns or verbs themselves ought to recur; for example, **Proverbs 9:7**, *he who corrects* <note>The text breaks here; the catchword indicates the word "corrects" (corripiens) continues on the next page.</note> a mocker...

[It] is constructed and joined with various other nouns, except that *se’et* <note>original Hebrew: שְׂאֵת; a noun form of the root *nasa* usually meaning "dignity" or "elevation."</note> sometimes takes on the force of a noun, specifically in **Genesis 49:3** and **Psalm 62:5**, as **Bertram** <note>Bonaventure Corneille Bertram (1531–1594), a notable Genevan Hebraist and theologian.</note> maintains. **First**, it is constructed with the word *blessing*, as in **Psalm 24:5**: *he shall receive a blessing from the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: יִשָּׂא בְרָכָה מֵאֵת יְהוָה (*yissa berakah me-et Yehovah*)</note>. **Secondly**, the same word means to pay the penalty for sin, whether for one's own sin—as in **Numbers 9:13**: *he shall bear his sin* <note>original Hebrew: יִשָּׂא חֶטְאוֹ (*yissa chet-o*)</note>—or for sin that is imputed <note>original Latin: *imputati*; a theological term referring to sin or righteousness assigned to someone else’s account.</note>, as when it is said of **Christ** by a certain metaphor in **Isaiah 53:4**: *he himself has borne our infirmities (our sins)* <note>original Hebrew: חֳלָיֵנוּ הוּא נָשָׂא (*cholayenu hu nasa*)</note>, as is immediately explained by the verb *to carry* <note>original Hebrew: סָבַל (*sabal*); a synonym for "to bear" often used for heavy burdens.</note>. And in **verse 8**, it is expressly read that *he paid the penalty for the transgression of the people*; that is, not because of his own stain, but because of a fault imputed from elsewhere. The prefix *be* <note>The Hebrew letter בְּ attached to the start of a word, often meaning "in" or "with."</note> hints at this meaning in **Ezekiel 18:20**: *The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father* <note>original Hebrew: לֹא יִשָּׂא בַּעֲוֺן הָאָב (*lo yissa be-avon ha-av*)</note>, *or the punishment for the sin committed by the father*. [The word] is constructed and joined with various other names, except that *se’et* <note>original Hebrew: שאת; the infinitive form of the verb *nasa* (to lift/bear), used here as a noun meaning "lifting up" or "excellence."</note> sometimes obtains the force of a noun, namely in **Genesis 49:3** and **Psalm 62:5**, as **Bertram** <note>Bonaventure Corneille Bertram (1531–1594), a Swiss Hebraist and professor.</note> contends. **First**, it is constructed with the word *blessing* <note>original Hebrew: ברכה (*berakhah*)</note>, as in **Psalm 24:5**: *he shall receive a blessing from the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: ישא ברכה מאת יהוה (*yissa berakhah me-et Yehovah*)</note>. At other times, it is joined with words denoting sin, specifically regarding the pardon of sin or the grace of an offense, as in **Exodus 34:7**, where God is said to be *forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin* <note>original Hebrew: נושא עון ופשע וחטאה (*nosei avon va-pesha ve-hata'ah*)</note>. In this case, a simple verb is used in place of a compound—a form which the Hebrew language lacks—namely, using "to bear" to mean "to bear away" <note>The author notes that Hebrew uses the simple verb *nasa* (to bear) to express the concept of the Latin *auferre* (to carry away/remove).</note>.

**Second**, the same word can mean to pay the penalty for sin, whether for one's own sin, as in **Numbers 9:13**: *he shall bear his sin* <note>original Hebrew: ישא חטאו (*yissa chet’o*)</note>, or for imputed sin, as when it is said of Christ through a certain metaphor in **Isaiah 53:4**: *he himself has borne our infirmities (sins)* <note>original Hebrew: חלינו הוא נשא (*kholayenu hu nasa*)</note>, as it is soon after explained by the word *sabal* <note>original Hebrew: סבל; a verb meaning to carry a heavy, burdensome load.</note>. And in **verse 8**, it is expressly read that he *paid the penalty* because of the transgression of the people; that is, not because of his own stain, but for a fault imputed from elsewhere. 

The prefixed letter *bet* <note>The Hebrew preposition ב typically meaning "in" or "with."</note> suggests this meaning in **Ezekiel 18:20**: *The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father* <note>original Hebrew: לא ישא בעון האב (*lo yissa be-avon ha-av*)</note>, or the punishment for the sin committed by the father. Indeed, it is explained thus in **Micah 7:9**: *I will bear the wrath of the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: זעף יהוה אשא (*za’af Yehovah essa*)</note>...

In Hebrew grammar, "servile" letters are those added to a root word to indicate gender, number, or tense. While this letter often marks a word as feminine, the author is arguing it is not an absolute rule.</note> are of the feminine gender, even if this is usually the case. Thus, it is established by a threefold argument that "sin" here is not of the feminine gender. XX. XXI. I grant, indeed, that the particle of similitude is sometimes missing, and thus must be supplied. For example, in *Psalm* 11:1, where David says: *I will hope in the Lord; how do you say to my soul, that it should flee from your mountain* [as a] *bird* <note>Hebrew: צִפּוֹר (*tsippor*)</note>? *This is* [understood as] *like a bird* <note>Hebrew: כְצִפּוֹר (*ke-tsippor*)</note>, *as Pagninus <note>Santes Pagnino (1470–1541), a prominent Italian Dominican Hebraist and Bible translator.</note> correctly supplied from Psalm 124:7.* Add also *Deuteronomy* 20:19, *Proverbs* 13:12, and *Psalm* 39:6. But where those passages are found, the text implies an ellipsis, and necessity even urges it; since disparate things cannot be predicated of each other in the nominative case <note>i.e., you cannot say "A is B" if A and B are totally different categories, so you must assume the meaning is "A is like B".</note>. But what necessity is there here, after all? It is also uncertain, as is supposed, that *crouching* is a term used properly only for quadrupeds. If we set aside the common concept from this discussion, it will appear that the erroneous deed itself is what is being signified, not the intended goal. (as it was said to Cain, "why are you angry and why has your countenance fallen?")* <note>original: *vultus tuus?* — The author uses the example of a sheep's natural instinct versus human choice to show that Cain's anger was a result of his will, not necessity.</note>

# BOOK I. MISCELLANEOUS [WORKS]

Let us therefore examine, as intended, what the sacred scriptures provide, and whether a "properly named" priesthood of Moses can be proven from *Psalm 99:6*, or if some other reasoning might be produced from those same scriptures to argue the point. The words of the Psalmist are these: <note>original Hebrew: "משה ואהרן בכהניו"</note> *Moses and Aaron were among his priests*. The *Chaldean* <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> renders it: *among his priests*; the *Syriac*: *among his priests*; the *Arabic*: *among his priests*. The *Latin*: *among his priests*. *Luther*: *Among his priests* <note>original German: "Unter seinen Priestern"</note>. The remaining Latin interpreters, except for *Osiander*, vary regarding the prefixed letter *Beth* <note>The Hebrew preposition "ב" (Beth) can mean "among," "with," or "in."</note>. The *Zurich scholars* <term>Tigurini: Scholars from Zurich who produced the Zurich Bible</term>, whom many commonly cite under the name of *Vatablus*, translated it: *among his priests*, that is, as the note by *Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, a French Hebraist</note> has it: *Moses and Aaron, the most illustrious of his priests*. *Junius and Tremellius* <note>Protestant biblical scholars famous for their Latin translation of the Old Testament</note> translate it: *Moses and Aaron with his priests, specifically, he [God] heard them*.

V. It is also the opinion of the Jews that Moses was a priest. Hence, in the *Michlal Jophi* <note>The "Perfection of Beauty," a commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> by the Rabbi who is called *Rabbi Samuel Tarfa* by Buxtorf, he writes on this passage concerning the word *among his priests*: <note>original Hebrew: "כי גם משה כהן והוא שמש בכהונה גדולה תחלה בשבעת ימי המלואים"</note> *it says* "among his priests" *because Moses also was a priest, and indeed the High Priest, at the beginning during the seven days of the consecration* <note>Referring to the seven days of the investiture of the Tabernacle and Aaron's family described in Leviticus 8.</note>. Similarly, *Abenezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a prominent medieval Jewish scholar</note> writes on this passage that the word <term>kohen: priest</term> in the entire sacred codex signifies a "minister of God," according to that passage of *Isaiah*—

VIII. XI. Thus, it should be known that the Hebrews elegantly use the accusative or ablative <note>The author is discussing how Hebrew uses different grammatical cases than Latin to express the "predicate"—what someone or something is.</note> in place of the nominative by using the <term>prefix Bet (ב)</term> <note>This is the "Beth Essentiae," a grammatical rule where the letter "B" is attached to a word to mean "as" or "in the capacity of."</note>, while the substantive verb "to be" (<term>hayah היה</term>) is suppressed. For example, in *Hosea* 13:10: <term>ki be’ezreka</term> <note>original: כִּי בְעֶזְרֶךָ; "for in your help"</note>. *Kimchi* <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, was a foundational medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator.</note> in his book *Michlol* <note>The *Sefer Michlol*, Kimchi’s famous work on Hebrew grammar.</note>, page 15, said this is placed instead of *ki ezreka* ["for [I am] your help"], meaning **your help is in me**. In *Psalm* 54:6: <term>Adonai be-somekhe nafshi</term> <note>original: אֲדֹנָי בְּסֹמְכֵי נַפְשִׁי</note>, **The Lord is among those who sustain my soul**, which means: **He is the sustainer of my soul**. From this, the Greeks rendered it: <note>original: ὁ κύριος ἀντιλήπτωρ τῆς ψυχῆς μου</note> **The Lord is the protector of my soul**. Likewise in *Psalm* 118:7: <term>Adonai li be-ozray</term> <note>original: אֲדֹנָי לִי בְּעֹזְרָי</note>, **The Lord is to me among my helpers**, that is, **He is my helper**; and thus the Greeks correctly translated it as: <note>original: ὁ κύριος ἐμοὶ βοηθός</note> **The Lord is my helper**. 

This same pattern of speech is frequent among the Arabs. For example: **God is** <note>original Arabic: بقدير (bi-qadir)</note> **in the powerful one**, that is, **He is powerful**. Or: **I am** <note>original Arabic: بمؤمن (bi-mu'min)</note> **in a believer**, that is, **I am believing** or **faithful**. However, when in Hebrew the <term>Bet (ב)</term> takes the place of <term>be-tokh</term> <note>original: בְּתוֹךְ; "in the midst of"</note>—that is, the prefix <term>Bet (ב)</term> denotes a middle position and signifies "among"—the Arabs are accustomed to use the particle <note>original Arabic: من (min)</note> ["from" or "out of"]. For example: **He is** <note>original Arabic: من الكاذبين (min al-kadhibin)</note> **out of the liars**, [meaning he is one of the liars].

## XI.
Thus, it may be noted that the Hebrews elegantly use the <term>accusative</term> <note>The grammatical case usually marking the direct object.</note> or <term>ablative</term> <note>The grammatical case usually marking separation or location.</note> in place of the nominative, using the <term>prefix</term> **beth** (ב) while the substantive verb *hayah* <note>The Hebrew verb "to be."</note> is suppressed or implied. ## XII.
Therefore, Juan de Pineda, a Spanish Jesuit, explains our opinion and the <term>equivocation</term> <note>The use of a single term to mean different things; in this case, "priest" versus "civil official."</note> of the word <note>original Hebrew: כֹּהֵן, *Cohen*</note>—even against the views of the rest—as follows: *“I admit that the name of 'priest' in the Scriptures does not always refer to a sacred and ecclesiastical office, but sometimes to a mark of honor and dignity (namely, used precisely to suggest any prince or excellent man). For although the word <note>original: כֹּהֵן, though Pineda suggests the verb form כִּהֵן, *kihen*, is more accurate here</note> properly signifies ministering in sacred matters, or being appointed to carry out sacred rites, it is nonetheless transferred from there to one who is a most intimate friend of some King or Prince, such as a secretary or a counselor. This is done while maintaining a proper sense of proportion and similarity. For just as priests are familiar with God and are most well-known and dear to Him, and those who deal with God concerning the most serious and secret matters; so indeed, since a King is a kind of God, and a certain appearance and representation of divine majesty and power, he who is most familiar and dear to the King seems to be a kind of priest.”* Thus says Pineda.

### XIV.

For, as I have said above, the King's power was restricted in both civil and sacred matters to such an extent that the Republic did not display the pure face of a Monarchy.

It is rather this that is absurd: to infer the force and meaning of Hebrew words from the usage of the Latin language, which is how Master P. trifles here with the word **priest**.

### CHAPTER V OF MISCELLANIES

XXIII. So much for the first example. **The second is read in 1 Kings 4:2**: <note>original Hebrew: *Ele ha-sarim asher lo Azaryahu ben-Tzadok ha-kohen*</note> "These were the officials who belonged to him [Solomon]: Azariahu son of Zadok, the priest." These are the princes—that is, the high officials—of Solomon; Azariahu, son of Zadok, was the primary official, or the one who stood above all other princes. On this point, **Vatablus** <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French scholar</note> correctly follows **Schindler**: translate this as "prince," and understand it to mean "chief of the princes," that is, the first among the officials of Solomon’s court. Indeed, it is not at all likely—given that the priesthood of Aaron was established—that under Solomon the same individuals served as both political princes and religious priests. This remains true even if those who were priests were admitted into the assembly known as the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme judicial and administrative council in ancient Israel</note> alongside their peers. For those who were admitted to that council were not "princes of the court," nor were they called priests for that reason, even though some among them were noblemen of venerable dignity.

### §. IX.
Nor should it be shrouded in silence that, by this very fact, Solomon is compared with other Kings who did not have so many wives. David, as <term>Drusius</term> <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616) was a highly influential Flemish Protestant scholar of the Old Testament and Hebrew.</note> testifies, had eight wives, to whom (if we believe the consensus of the Jewish scholars) eighteen were granted by divine law. ### §. XI. 
But for me, these arguments are not yet sufficient. A unanimous consensus of lexicographers is owed to the Scripture, which does not use words otherwise than how you find them explained there. **Rabbi Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, was a preeminent medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> in his *Lexicon*, and following him, the **Michlol Yophi** <note>A "Perfection of Beauty," a commentary on the Hebrew Bible by Solomon ibn Melech, published in the 16th century.</note> on chapter 25, verse 6 of Genesis, describe a **concubine** <note>original Hebrew: פלגש (*pilegesh*)</note> as follows: **a handmaid set apart for a man for his bed without a marriage contract and without sanctification** <note>original Hebrew: אָמָה הַמְּיוּחֶדֶת לְאָדָם לְמִשְׁכָּבוֹ בְּלֹא כְּתוּבָה וּבְלֹא קִדּוּשִׁין. A <term>Ketubah</term> is a formal marriage contract, while <term>Kiddushin</term> refers to the formal betrothal process.</note>; that is, *a handmaid joined to a man so that she might lie with him, yet without the letters of dowry and solemn nuptials.* He repeats and emphasizes the same point in his **commentary** <note>original Hebrew: פירש (*perush*)</note> on 2 Samuel 5:13, and adds that according to very ancient custom, **concubines** <note>original Hebrew: פלגשים (*pilegeshim*)</note> are distinguished from **wives** <note>original Hebrew: נשים (*nashim*)</note>, because the latter celebrated their nuptials **with a marriage contract and sanctification**, *under the provision of dowry documents and solemn betrothals.* To which point we should refer the fact that since the sons of concubines were by no means heirs, nor did they enjoy such legal documents, they had to be content with gifts, as seen in **Genesis 25:6**.

## [MISCELLANEOUS] CHAPTER VI.

**XLIX, 4.** David took in Jerusalem **concubines** <note>original Hebrew: פִּלַגְשִׁים (*pilegeshim*)</note> and **wives** <note>original Hebrew: נָשִׁים (*nashim*)</note> (whom Absalom later defiled <note>This refers to the events of 2 Samuel 16:21–22, where Absalom publicly lay with his father’s concubines to assert his claim to the throne.</note>) and from them he fathered sons and daughters, *2 Samuel 5:13*. Solomon, following in the footsteps of his parent, also multiplied wives and concubines, but more than was just. Indeed, wherever a mention of concubines exists in opposition to wives, the children who are immediately mentioned in the text prove that these are understood not to be virgins, but women who have known men <note>original: *maritatas*—literally "married," but here implying women who have entered into a sexual union</note>.

### §. XIII. 
Nor do the cited passages stand in the way. For in the former passage, **concubines** <note>original: פִּלַגְשִׁים</note> are not distinguished in contrast to **wives** <note>original: נָשִׁים</note>. Therefore, even if the word in that single passage—as **Luther**, **Tremellius**, and **Buxtorf** <note>Martin Luther (the Reformer), Immanuel Tremellius (a converted Jewish Hebraist), and Johannes Buxtorf (a leading 17th-century Christian Hebraist) were all influential scholars of the Hebrew Bible.</note> were convinced—were taken to refer to the female sex in general, it still could not be applied to our controversy, where a distinction is established between them. Whenever such an opposition occurs, it implies not merely an empty harem <note>original: *Gynæceum*</note>, but women who have experienced men. Without a doubt, 700 women—whether virgins or royal wives—would have had at least as many handmaids, not just three hundred; thus the harem would have consisted of far more persons.

### §. XIV. 
Nor is it unusual for the same word to signify sometimes only the sex, and sometimes also the status of the person, as the predicates <note>the grammatical context or descriptors attached to the word</note> demand...

§. II. Furthermore, regarding what the Jewish people <note>original: <term>Recutiti</term>, a Latin term literally meaning "the circumcised," often used in historical texts to refer to Jews.</note> suppose, Christians are by no means in agreement among themselves; thus a dispute has arisen as to whether polygamy was permitted not only to the Patriarchs but also to the Jews, or even granted by law, so that they might be excused in the **court of heaven** <note>original: <term>forum poli</term>; a theological term for God's judgment or the spiritual realm, as opposed to earthly courts.</note>, as they say. Martin Luther clearly indicates what he thinks, both in his commentary on *Genesis chapter 16* and in his *disputation on the Digamy of Bishops, section 65.* He believes that the law of the brother <note>Referring to the "Levirate" law (Yibbum), where a man was required to marry his deceased brother's childless widow.</note> explicitly requires simultaneous polygamy, assuming that the younger brother was already bound in marriage. So that they may explain this more clearly elsewhere, they argue especially in this way: ***That which God commands is not intrinsically a sin. God commanded polygamy.***

The Laws are numbered as <term>613</term> <note>original Hebrew: תריג (*Taryag*), the numerical value of the 613 commandments in the Torah.</note>. Therefore, lest this infamous reproach for neglecting the law diminish the King's authority—whether he was to receive the spit or reject it—it seemed right to the elders that this should be granted to the King’s honor, so that in this matter he might be viewed differently from the rest.

Although <term>brothers</term> <note>original Hebrew: אחים (*achim*)</note> may be spoken of in a more general sense, both the father of Abraham had died long ago, and God had given him a command, *chapter 12:1*, to leave his home and kinship and seek Palestine. Therefore, those who are said to *dwell together* are not necessarily confined to a shared building, much less their father's, but rather live within a certain *geographical* distance or a specific range.

XI. *R. Salomo* <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, or Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> claims that those who "dwell together" are those whose general residence is in this world <note>i.e., they are contemporaries, living at the same time</note>; and if those brothers were co-heirs, the widow’s assets are not taken into account. Thus, there is no suspicion here that the brothers must live in their father's house. Different families of brothers can live in separate houses while the father is still alive; they can also stay in the same house after his death, particularly if one is unmarried, yet the house is by no means required to be the father’s. Respect was rightly paid to the inheritance or possession of the Jews: so that it would never be divided or, through repeated marriages, completely lost to the tribe. A similar law exists regarding both sexes, found in *Numbers 36:7 and 8*.

<meta>This page continues the critique of the Greek Septuagint's influence on later biblical translations and theological arguments. It specifically examines how Saint Jerome, despite his Hebrew scholarship, occasionally relied on flawed Greek renderings when debating the Pelagians.</meta>

<page-num>127.</page-num>
<header>GREEK [TEXTS] CHAPTER VIII.</header>

...the Greek [version] to such an extent that he not infrequently followed it in controversies as if it were a kind of standard. *Saint Jerome*, <note>original: "S. Hieronymus"; the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate</note> who was highly learned in Hebrew, provides us with an example in his *Letter to Ctesiphon*, written against the *Pelagians*: <note>The Pelagians were followers of Pelagius, who argued that humans could achieve moral perfection through their own will without divine grace. Jerome wrote this letter to refute them.</note> *“If the commandments are easy,”* he says, *“bring forward someone who has fulfilled them, and tell us why David sings in the Psalm: ‘You who fashion toil into the commandment?’ and again: ‘Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways.’”* These are his words.

Certainly, neither passage serves to prove his point. The first is found in *Psalm 94:20*; it does not speak of God or His law, but of the throne of a tyrant, who, by his own authority, imposes all kinds of afflictions and troubles upon the people contrary to God's command. We encounter the second in *Psalm 17:4*, where the Greeks incorrectly translated the text. For the Hebrew here has: <note>original Hebrew: אֲנִי שָׁמַרְתִּי אָרְחוֹת פָּרִיץ / ani shamarti orchot paritz</note> *“I have observed (or avoided) the ways of the violent man [or the sinner].”* <term>Symmachus</term> <note>An early 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek known for clarity.</note> renders it: *“of the transgressor.”* <note>original Greek: παραβάτου</note> The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The most influential ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> translates: *“I have kept hard ways.”* <note>original Greek: ἐφύλαξα ὁδοὺς σκληράς</note> There is no mention here of divine law, but rather of the "ways of the wicked," which we ought to turn away from.

He writes: <note>original Latin: "nolentem prævenit, ut velit: volentem subsequitur, ne frustra velit."</note> *It precedes the unwilling that they may will; it follows the willing, lest they will in vain.* Here he followed the Greeks, who err in two ways. They translated it as: <note>original Greek: ὁ θεός µε, τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ προφθάσει µε</note> *God, His mercy shall precede me.* It is as if they had read: <note>original Hebrew: אֱלֹהַי חַסְדּוֹ</note> *Elohay chasdo* [My God, His mercy] or *Elohay* [My God], whereas it should be read as <note>original Hebrew: אֱלֹהַי חַסְדִּי</note> *Elohay chasdi*, which means *The God of my mercy shall precede me*, as the Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars who compiled the authoritative Hebrew text and provided marginal notes to preserve correct pronunciation and reading.</note> advise in the margin, just as what follows says: *God shall make me look upon [my enemies].* Similarly, in *Psalm 27:10*, it is said: <note>original Hebrew: אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׁעִי</note> *The God of my salvation.* Nor do I see any reason why we should place the name of God in the nominative case on its own when a more suitable grammatical construction is available. The *Syriac* and *Arabic* versions treat the word *God* as a vocative <note>A case used for direct address, i.e., "O God."</note> and translate the text as if they had read *His mercy*.

§. IX. Let that be the opinion of the Jews, and let the Greeks follow it: but no necessity compels us to think that almsgiving is denoted by the word *righteousness* <note>original Hebrew: צדקה (*tsedakah*)</note>, which by the most widely accepted usage signifies justice or righteousness. For besides the fact that the act of redemption denoted by such words refers to a person [being ransomed] and not to a specific work—much less the privation of a work—this passage is certainly dealing with the conversion of a human being. Finally, while others explain the passage as referring to the punishment for sin—which they say is removed or at least mitigated by the amendment of one's life—*Chamier* <note>Daniel Chamier (1565–1621), a prominent French Reformed theologian and author of the *Panstratia Catholica*.</note> denies that "sin" is ever used to mean "punishment" <note>original Latin: *peccatum sumi pro poenâ*</note>, and thus he condemns the writers of the previous century for their ignorance. His reasoning is that since the word "sin" often occurs in place of a "sacrifice" <note>In biblical Hebrew, the word *chattat* can mean both "sin" and "sin-offering."</note>—that is, the transfer of sin and the forgiveness of punishment—it cannot, by contrast, be used to mean the punishment itself. The Hebrew reads: *gadol avoni minso* <note>original Hebrew: גדול עוני מנשא</note>, which means: *my punishment is greater than I can bear*. This is the view held by *Junius, Drusius, Piscator, Sixtinus Amama*, and others. One might rather attribute that "ignorance" to *Chamier* himself: for in Zechariah 14:19, the word is explicitly used for punishment, when it says: *zot tihyeh chattat mitsrayim ve-chattat kol ha-goyim* <note>original Hebrew: זאת תהיה חטאת מצרים וחטאת כל הגוים</note>, meaning: *this shall be the punishment of Egypt and the punishment of all nations*. XXIII. To perceive this more correctly, especially regarding the words of the Apostle cited from *Romans 1:23 and 25*, a few points should be noted in passing. 1. Those who, along with Hofmann <note>Johann Wilhelm Hofmann (1676–1739), a scholar previously cited as holding a different view on the corruption of the divine concept</note>, cling only to the bare words, interpret the text incorrectly. They explain the "changing" of one thing into another in such a way as if truth itself passes into a lie, or glory into shame. They ought to have weighed the phrase, which carries the flavor of Hebrew idiom. For the word **exchanged** <note>original Hebrew: המיר (*hamir*)</note>, when constructed with the preposition **with** <note>original: בְּ (*be*)</note>, does not only mean *to change a certain thing so that it becomes something else*, but also *to exchange it with another thing*, which is otherwise expressed by the word **to substitute** <note>original Hebrew: החליף (*hachaliph*)</note>. For example, in *Leviticus 27:10*: *he shall not exchange it, a good for a bad or a bad for a good* <note>original Hebrew: הֵמִיר טוֹב בְּרָע אוֹ רָע בְּטוֹב (*hemir tov be-ra o ra be-tov*)</note>. The sense here is that he exchanged or bartered a good item for a bad one, or a bad one for a good one; it does not mean that he literally "changed the good into a bad thing." Likewise, in *Psalm 106:20*: *they exchanged their glory for the image of an ox that eats grass* <note>original Hebrew: וַיָּמִירוּ כְבוֹדָם בְּתַבְנִית שׁוֹר אֹכֵל עֵשֶׂב (*vayamiro kevodam be-tavnit shor ochel esev*)</note>, which means they exchanged their glory (meaning God, who is called the Glory of Israel) with the likeness of an ox eating grass—an allusion to the events in *Exodus 32*. See also *Jeremiah 2:11* and *Hosea 4:7*.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.

->*It is shown that there is a need for caution, lest we easily assert anything universally in Sacred Philology, and this is confirmed by the provided examples.*<-

**I.** The Ancients <note>Refers to the Church Fathers or early scholars.</note> spoke both learnedly and cautiously: *let the fall of the great not be the delight of the lesser, but let the fall of the great be the trembling of the lesser.* Nor do we, who carefully investigate the sayings of others everywhere, take such delight in their errors as if our intention were to disparage most distinguished men; rather, we deem it necessary to give a public warning so that we do not strike our own foot against the same stone they did. 

Let our first example be those who, in the examination of the passage in **Acts 3:21**, claim that the word *dechomai* <note>original Greek: τὸ δέχομαι, meaning "to receive" or "to welcome"</note> is always taken **actively** <note>original Greek: ἐνεργητικῶς (*energetikōs*)</note>, as they put it, but never **passively**. Indeed—

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the name "Machpelah" from Genesis 23. While the previous page introduced Claude Salmasius’s skepticism regarding the traditional "double cave" interpretation, this page offers a rebuttal, arguing that "Machpelah" is a proper geographical place name rather than a descriptive adjective.</meta>

160.
<header>BOOK I. MISCELLA[NIES]</header>

III. I do not listen to this "Dictator" <note>The author refers to Claude Salmasius (1588–1653), a dominant figure in 17th-century classical scholarship, as a "Dictator" of letters.</note>, but think an entirely different opinion must be sought. My reasoning is twofold. 1. Because, just as the cave is so named, the field is also called the **field of Machpelah** <note>original Hebrew: המכפלה, *ha-Machpelah*</note>, in verse 19. If the cave is called **Machpelah** <note>Hebrew root *kaphal* means "to double."</note> because of a double opening or aperture—or, if I may say so, a double gate—in what sense will the field itself be called the "field of Machpelah"? Will you attribute a double gate to the field as well? 2. Because in verse 17, the cave is said to have been **in Machpelah before Mamre** <note>original Hebrew: במכפלה לפני ממרא, *be-Machpelah liphnei Mamre*</note>, that is, in a specific place that was across from Mamre.

IV. Therefore, it is rightly established that **Machpelah** is the name of a place. And it is most correctly called the "cave of Machpelah" and the "field of Machpelah," because both the former and the latter were located in that region which was called Machpelah. Nor is it a new thing for proper names, whether of people or of places, to be interpreted as common nouns by translators, and vice versa.

Thus, the **Latin Vulgate** <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible which became the standard for the Catholic Church.</note> translator, in **1 Chronicles 4:22**, translates the proper name **Jokim** <note>original Hebrew: יוקים</note> as **he who made the sun stand still** <note>original Latin: *qui stare fecit solem*</note>. Likewise, the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> at **Amos chapter 1, verse 6**, lacking the vowel points <note>Ancient Hebrew was written without vowels; later scholars added "points" to clarify pronunciation. Without them, words with the same consonants can be confused.</note>, translate **a full captivity** <note>original Hebrew: גלות שלמה, *galut shelemah*</note> as **the captivity of Solomon** <note>original Greek: αἰχμαλωσίαν τοῦ Σολομὼν, *aichmalōsian tou Solomōn*</note>, as if they had read the name **Solomon** <note>original Hebrew: שלמה, *Sh'lomoh*</note>. In **Judges 8:13**, where the text has **from the ascent of the sun** <note>original Hebrew: מלמעלה החרס, *mi-ma'aleh ha-chares*</note>—that is, "before the rising of the sun"—they rendered it: **by the ascent of Heres** <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ ἀναβάσεως Ἁρές, *hypo anabaseōs Ares*</note>.
