<header>[MISCELLA]NEOUS CHAPTER I.</header>

V. It does not matter that the [Hebrew letter] *He* <note>The letter ה (*he*) in Hebrew often serves as the definite article "the."</note> is prefixed to the word Machpelah <note>original Hebrew: מכפלה</note>, nor that this article does not otherwise apply to proper names. For there is one rule for names that are proper to persons, and another for those that belong to specific places. Likewise, even in the names of persons, the prefixed *He* has a place if they are also common nouns <note>term: *appellativa* — words that describe a category of thing rather than a specific individual name.</note>, or indeed could be so; for example, in **Numbers 3:21**, mention is made of the "family of the Shimeites" <note>original Hebrew: משפחת השמעי, *mishpahat ha-Shimei*</note>, the family of Shimei. Furthermore, there are place names [with this prefix], such as **Hachilah**, **the Jeshimon**, and **Gibeah** <note>original Hebrew: החכילה (*ha-Hachilah*), הישימון (*ha-Jeshimon*), הגבעה (*ha-Gibeah*)</note> in **1 Samuel 26:1, 3** and **chapter 23:19**.

<header>BOOK II. MISCELLANEOUS</header>

...that common saying, *nothing in excess* <note>original Latin: *ne quid nimis* — a famous classical proverb advocating for moderation in all things.</note>: so it must be carefully investigated in what manner we should accept what the wisest of mortals <note>Referring to King Solomon, the traditional author of Ecclesiastes.</note> asserts to be possible. There is more than one Jewish opinion regarding the meaning of this saying, and various applications of it. *Maimonides* <note>A preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> in *Hilchot De’ot* <note>original Hebrew: הלכות דעות (*Hilkhot De'ot*), "Laws of Character Traits" or "Ethics."</note>, *or the Treatise on Knowledge, chapter 3, adapts it as follows:* "The Sages have forbidden a man from afflicting himself with fasting, and regarding all these things and similar matters Solomon commanded and said: *Do not be righteous overmuch*" <note>original Hebrew: אל-תהי צדיק הרבה (*al-tehi tzaddik harbeh*)</note>. That is to say: *The Rabbis forbade anyone to devote more effort than is right to fasting and other similar things (namely, that he should not abstain excessively from meat and wine, from clothing, marriage, and other lawful things); for concerning these Solomon spoke and commanded, "do not be righteous overmuch." He clearly shows that a sin is committed on both sides: both if one indulges his own will more than is right and follows lust against God’s law, and conversely, if he wishes to abstain so much from even lawful things that he utterly turns away from meat, wine, a wife, and even permitted clothing. Therefore, one must walk the straight path and tread the middle way.* <note>term: *media via* — the "Golden Mean," a philosophical concept where virtue exists as a balance between two extremes.</note>

II. *In the Book of the Pious* <note>original Hebrew: ספר חסידים (*Sefer Hasidim*), a 12th/13th-century Hebrew text on ethics and piety.</note>, *number 831, this story is recounted, through which the Jews strive to show the interpretation of this passage:* "There were two men; one did not want to burn [kill] flies. His companion said to him: *Do not be righteous* [overmuch]..."

**...Too righteous; it is better to burn flies so that they do not fall into food and drink.** <note>original Hebrew: צַדִּיק הַרְבֵּה מוּטָב לִשְׂרֹף זְבוּבִים כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִפְּלוּ בְּמַאֲכָל וּבְמִשְׁתֶּה</note> That is to say: there were two individuals, one of whom did not dare to even burn flies; he received this response from his companion: *Do not be righteous overmuch.* It is entirely better to have burned the flies than for them to fall into food and drink, and for us to perhaps commit a sin by swallowing them <note>In Jewish dietary law (Kashrut), consuming insects is a violation; the anecdote suggests that "mercy" toward a fly leads to the greater "sin" of eating it.</note>.

This Jew was not unlike a certain Hermit who thought it was cautioned in the fifth commandment <note>original Latin: *præceptô quintô* — in the numbering system used by the author, likely following the Augustinian tradition, the prohibition "Thou shalt not kill" is the fifth commandment. In other traditions, it is the sixth.</note> that no one should kill even fleas or other insects.

Furthermore, in number 405 of the same book, another history or fable is recounted. Namely, they claim there existed a certain woman named *Shitraya* <note>original Hebrew: שִׁטְרַיָּא</note>, whom the Hebrews call a *sorceress* <note>original Hebrew: מְכַשֵּׁפָה (*mekhashefah*) — a term for a practitioner of magic or witchcraft.</note>, who had affected a Jew with loss and injury—indeed, to such an extent that the matter could no longer be kept secret. According to Jewish tradition, her life could not be prolonged unless on the following day she shared **of his morsel and his salt** <note>original Hebrew: מִפִּתּוֹ וּמִמֶּלַח שֶׁלוֹ (*mi-pito u-mi-melach shelo*). In many cultures, sharing bread and salt creates a bond of hospitality and protection.</note>—that is, of his bread and salt. When she sought this, a certain Apella <note>term: *Apella* — a name used by the Roman poet Horace to refer to a typical Jew; here it denotes a Jewish elder.</note>, venerable in age, rebuked the Jew who might have granted it by citing this very passage: *namely, that he should not be righteous overmuch.* For it could easily happen that if she shared in the bread and salt, her life would be prolonged, and she would thus perform even more evil.

IV. In **Augustine’s** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD). The work cited, *Questions on the Old Testament*, is a collection of biblical commentaries.</note> *Questions sought from the Old Testament*, this is the opinion: *Since the law declares one to be just, and he is truly just who possesses full justice, how then does Solomon say the opposite: "do not be righteous overmuch"? For he who is "much just" is not without malice, because if you respond to every single sin of those who err, you will not fail to sin yourself. Finally, God’s justice is tempered. For the Law, because it cannot soften itself, must be mitigated by us, so that it might be able to benefit those acting under it. Here, therefore, he is not "just overmuch" who is an imitator of God.*

V. **Joseph Hall**, Dean of Worcester <note>Joseph Hall (1574–1656) was an English bishop, satirist, and moralist, often called the "English Seneca" for his prose style.</note>, a man praised as "most illustrious" in the 16th session of the **Synod of Dort** <note>The Synod of Dort (1618–1619) was an international assembly of the Reformed Church held in the Netherlands to settle a theological dispute regarding predestination.</note>, is said to have written a most precise exhortation on this passage, so much so that thanks were given to him in the name of the National Synod. Therefore, in the cited place, after he had recited verses 15, 16, and 20 of the controversial chapter, he adds: *Justice is absolute; in this way, no one is just. Justice is begun <note>original: "inchoata" — referring to the partial righteousness believers achieve in this life through grace.</note> in its own kind; in this way, the just man perishes. Justice is equivocal; in this way, do not be overmuch just.* 

He distinguishes this "equivocal" <note>In this context, Hall means a "false" or "ambiguous" righteousness that appears to be virtue but is not.</note> justice in such a way that, according to it, some are "overmuch just" in their own opinion—such as the **Papists** <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics.</note>, who boast of works of **supererogation** <note>The doctrine that it is possible to do more good works than God’s law requires.</note>. Others, in actual practice, strive too much for a certain kind of justice, and this either publicly or privately. 

Publicly, this includes those who follow the very rigor of the law in judging a little too severely, while neglecting every consideration of **equity** <note>original Greek: "ἐπιεικείας" (epieikeia) — a legal concept meaning the correction of a law where it is defective owing to its universality; mercy or fairness.</note>. It also includes those interpreters of the sacred law who are accustomed to enslave themselves to letters and syllables in such a way as if the divine meaning were not in the **marrow** <note>original: "medulla" — the core or spirit of the text.</note> but on the surface. Or, on the other hand, it includes those who fashion a "prodigious" justice for **God**—one that should not even be heard by pious ears. 

Privately, he says that those who are "equivocally overmuch just" are those who either avoid things lawfully granted to us, or who affect an excessive degree of **holiness**— <note>The text cuts off here at "san-", continued by the catchword "ctimonia" (sanctimonia) on the following page.</note>

VI. But this "accurate"—as it is called—declaration neither agrees with itself, nor entirely achieves what it intends, even if it is not false in every respect. For it confuses things that ought to be distinguished. Privately and in actual practice, it calls those "just" who affect a holiness that has nowhere been commanded; and such was that opinion of the Pharisee in **Luke 18** <note>In the Parable of the Pharisee and the Tax Collector, the Pharisee boasts of his own religious observances as a form of self-righteousness.</note>. It mixes controversies of justice into the discussion beyond the scope of the text, since a person who understands everything according to the letter is not "too just," but rather "wise" in his own eyes. Finally, such "prodigious justice" does not even deserve the name of justice. 

This is my opinion, which is also approved by **Blessed Martin Luther** and **Conrad Pellican** <note>Conrad Pellican (1478–1556) was a pioneering Protestant reformer and Hebrew scholar.</note>, and can be confirmed by the consensus of the text itself: namely, the discourse here is not concerning that justice which they call "universal" (which is nothing other than a certain complex of all virtues. In this way, we are said to have been created in justice before the **state of the Fall** <note>original: *status lapsus* — the theological condition of humanity after the first sin of Adam and Eve, contrasted here with the original "universal justice" of creation.</note>), but rather concerning "particular justice." This "particular justice" consists in judgments, whether they regard Ecclesiastical or Political censure. Furthermore, that observation of **Augustine** must be entirely observed: *The Law, because it cannot soften itself, must be mitigated by us*; likewise that other proverb: *Extreme law is extreme...* <note>original: *summum jus* — the author is referencing the legal maxim *summum jus, summa injuria*, meaning "extreme law is extreme injustice." This suggests that a rigid, literal application of the law without equity leads to unfairness.</note>

## BOOK II. CHAPTER II.

### *Some Observations on the Restriction of Universal Expressions.*

I have read elsewhere about **universal expressions** <note>terms like "all," "none," or "every" which apply to an entire group</note>, and I have discussed at length how they are primarily expressed by the **Hebrews**, as far as paper and leisure then allowed. Now, some additions must be made, which it will be useful to have noted for our purpose. Unless I am completely mistaken, I proved in **Disquisition I on Sacred Expressions** <note>original: *Disp. I. de Loc. Sacr.*</note> that the word "all" <note>original: *omne*</note> is foolishly restricted by the word "many" <note>original: *πολλῶν* (pollōn)</note>; I will hereafter demonstrate that others fall into the same absurdity when they devise certain other restrictions.

There are times when a certain exception is found within the Sacred Code itself. Hence, in *John 1:3*, it is said of Christ: *All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made, that which was made.* <note>The author provides both the Greek *ὃ γέγονε* and Latin *quod factum est* for "that which was made."</note> For those who formerly either divided the text or transformed "nothing" into "something" were not in their right minds. Sin, indeed, was not made through him, and it is clear that sin is nothing, and men become nothing...”*

In the Scriptures, the phrase **from the rising of the sun to its setting** <note>original Hebrew: מִמִּזְרַח־שֶׁמֶשׁ וְעַד־מְבוֹאוֹ (*mi-mizrach-shemesh ve-ad-mewo’o*)</note> denotes the entire expanse of the earth through <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech in which a part is used to represent the whole, or vice versa</note>, even though **North** <note>original Hebrew: צָפוֹן (*tzafon*)</note> and **South** <note>original Hebrew: דָּרוֹם (*darom*)</note> are not specifically listed. For example, in *Malachi 1:11*: *From the rising of the sun even to its going down, my name is great among the nations* <note>original Latin: *ab ortu Solis usque in occasum ejus magnum est nomen meum inter gentes*</note>; that is, in the entire habitable world. For although **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish rabbi and biblical commentator</note> thinks this refers to the fact that the **inhabited world** <note>original Hebrew: הַיִּשּׁוּב (*ha-yishuv*); original Greek: οἰκουμένη (*oikoumene*)</note>—the land lived upon from East to West—serves man for his sustenance and dwelling in its entirety, whereas the situation is different regarding the North and South; it is nevertheless a synecdoche, since there are also those in those regions who celebrate the name of <term>GOD</term>.

VI. **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers</note> noted the same thing regarding the words **Heaven** <note>original Hebrew: שָׁמַיִם (*shamayim*)</note> and **Earth** <note>original Hebrew: אֶרֶץ (*eretz*)</note>, in *Volume 4, Question 5 on Deuteronomy*, with these words: *In that which is written, "God made heaven and earth," we must also understand the waters. For the Scripture, by naming these two parts, frequently intends for the whole world to be understood according to that phrase: "Who made heaven and earth," and countless others of this kind.* <note>original Latin: *In eo, quod scriptum est, fecit DEUS cœlum & terram, & aquas debemus accipere. Assiduè quippe Scriptura his duabus partibus commemoratis universum mundum vult intelligi...*</note> See the following passages: *Genesis 2:1, chapter 14:19; Psalm 69:35, Psalm 146:6, Psalm 121:2; Isaiah 45:2; Jeremiah 11:11; Jonah 1:9; Acts 4:24; Revelation 14:7.*

VII. Therefore, it is by no means a restriction when mention is made of heaven and earth, but sometimes an "amplification" <note>a rhetorical expansion or emphasis</note>, as can be seen in the passages cited.

...it happens, and whether the context itself indicates that things which ought to be understood specifically should not be taken in an absolute sense. For example, in **Mark 16:15**, we read the Savior’s decree given to the Apostles: *Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel* **to every creature.** <note>original Greek: πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει (*pásē tēi ktísei*); original Latin: *omni creaturæ*.</note> Therefore, should it be preached even to cows, sheep, geese, and other beasts? Although "those who enter the world" <note>Hebrew: בָּאֵי עוֹלָם (*ba'ei olam*)</note> is a general expression, it is understood specifically in the New Testament to mean humans. Thus, in **John 1:9** and elsewhere, the phrase **to come into the world** means **to be born.**

...following in their footsteps. These men assert that in **Romans 8:22**, "every creature" should likewise be understood as referring to humanity alone, no less than in **Colossians 1:15**, where our Savior is called the **firstborn of every creature.** <note>original Greek: πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως (*prōtotokos pasēs ktiseōs*); original Latin: *primogenitus omnis creaturæ*.</note> The Calvinists of Leiden <note>Refers to theologians at the University of Leiden in the Netherlands, a center of intense Reformed theological debate in the 17th century.</note> provided the occasion for this view, as they exempt not only man, but even the **system of the world** itself from the substantial destruction that is to come at the end of the world.

However, although the phrase, when considered in isolation, might not reject that meaning, the division of "creature" into specific underlying categories established in the text of **Colossians 1:16** stands in the way. For in that passage, He is called the firstborn of every creature for this reason: because through Him all things were created—those in the heavens and those on earth—that is, absolutely all things, visible and invisible, including even the "thrones" and "dominions," which refers to the **ranks of angels.** <note>original Latin: *angelorum ordines*. The author argues that since "creature" here includes angels and celestial things, it cannot mean "humanity alone."</note> 

And in **Romans 8**, the contrast made in the text also stands in the way of that narrow interpretation. For the "creature" mentioned there is said to "anxiously await" the revelation of the **sons of God** (verse 19), and is said to be eventually "liberated from the bondage of corruption" at the same time the sons of God are liberated (verse 21). Indeed, the Apostle Paul moves by a process of gradation from the irrational creature to the sons of God, and from these specifically to those who had received the "firstfruits of the Spirit." <note>The author is pointing out that because the "creature" is waiting for "humanity" (the sons of God), the "creature" must be something else—likely the natural world or the physical cosmos.</note>

XVII. What do the **Remonstrants** <term>Remonstrants: A group of Dutch Protestants who followed the teachings of Jacobus Arminius; they were often at odds with strict Calvinist orthodoxy regarding predestination and grace.</term> say to these things? They deny that there is any opposition of subjects here. Thus, when verse 19 says, *the creature waits for the revelation of the sons of GOD*, they interpret it in such a sense that the (new) creature expects its own revelation. They claim this is a <term>Hebraism: A grammatical structure or idiom typical of the Hebrew language that persists when translated into Greek or Latin.</term>. For the Hebrews not infrequently place the antecedent noun in the place of a relative pronoun, as seen in **1 Kings 8:1**, **Genesis 1:27**, **chapter 5:1**, **1 Samuel 3:21**, and **chapter 25:22**. <note>The author is pointing out a quirk where a sentence might say "God created man in the image of God" instead of "in His own image."</note> New Testament passages are also cited: **1 Corinthians 1:8**, **2 Thessalonians 3:5**, and **2 Timothy 1:18**.

Nor do they think they are devoid of reason; rather, they boast that their reasoning is manifest. For they argue it is absurd to attribute to the "old creature" <note>Referring to the natural world or non-believers.</note> that it waits for the revelation of the sons of GOD "with head outstretched" <note>original Latin: *exerto capite*. This translates the Greek word *apokaradokia*, implying a person craning their neck to see something coming.</note>, or that it hopes for liberation from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of GOD. On the contrary, they believe all these things are best attributed to the pious and the faithful. Thus, they claim nothing at all opposes this exposition: not the phrasing (which is made clear by the Hebraism), nor the word *creation* <note>original Greek: κτίσεως (*ktiseōs*)</note> being used on its own, because the "new creature" is simply called "creature" *preeminently* <note>original Greek: κατ' ἐξοχήν (*kat' exochēn*)</note>, as in **Colossians 1:15**, **Ephesians 2:10**, **James 1:18**, and **Revelation 3:14**.

### CHAPTER II. OF MISCELLANIES

For the rule of the Hebrews is fully cited by the **Remonstrants**. To be sure, they place the antecedent <note>The noun to which a later word refers.</note> in the position of the relative pronoun, but they do so with a noun that had already appeared earlier in the same text. For example, **Genesis 4:23**: <note>original Hebrew: וַיֹּאמֶר לֶמֶךְ לְנָשָׁיו שְׁמַעַן קוֹלִי נְשֵׁי לֶמֶךְ</note> *And Lamech said to his wives: Hear my voice, you wives of Lamech.* <note>Instead of saying "my wives," the text repeats the name: "wives of Lamech."</note> This same point is proven both by other examples and by those very ones brought forward by the Remonstrants.

There is only one passage that has slightly changed the antecedent, and we encounter it in **2 Thessalonians 3:5**, where it is said: *The Lord* <note>Greek: κύριος (*Kyrios*)</note> *direct your hearts into the love of God* <note>Greek: τοῦ θεοῦ (*tou theou*)</note>—that is, of himself—*and into the expectation of Christ.* But here, there is a very serious reason why the antecedent was changed: the style of the New Testament, in which St. Paul (following **Psalm 110:1**) is accustomed to call Christ "Lord," and the Father "God," as is evident from **1 Corinthians 8:6** and **Ephesians 1:2**. In these passages, the persons of the Deity are compared or joined together. This is done both so that no one might conceive of there being multiple Gods, and because he attributes specific <term>distinguishing marks: Known in Greek as γνωρίσματα (*gnorismata*); these are the unique characteristics used to identify or tell apart the different persons of the Trinity.</term> to each person, by which one may be distinguished from the other.

As in **1 Corinthians 12:4, 5, 6**, Paul himself shows this with these words: *there are differences of graces* <note>Often translated as "spiritual gifts."</note>, *but the same Spirit; and there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are differences of operations*...

XXI. Next, we must consider what kind of matter is being discussed. For it is either known by nature, or it is established solely by revelation. If it is known to us naturally and rests on firm reasons, we must then take care, first, that we do not mix anything into this whole subject that exceeds our reason, and second, that the proposition is not extended further than the matter itself allows. **For Augustine rightly says in Volume 2, Letter 7 to Marcellinus:**

> *If a reason is given against the authority of the divine scriptures, however sharp it may be, it deceives by its likeness to truth; for it cannot be true. On the other hand, if the authority of the Holy Scriptures is held up as an objection against a manifest and certain reason, the person who does this does not understand; he is not setting the sense of those scriptures—which he could not penetrate—against the truth, but rather his own sense; he opposes the truth not with what he found in the scriptures, but with what he found in himself as if it were on their behalf.*

XXIII. **Lombard** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1164), author of the *Sentences*, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> is likewise mistaken here. Aquinas is making a subtle distinction: the process applies to all food types generally, but does not mean 100% of the matter is expelled.</note>. To this opinion **Maldonatus** <note>Juan de Maldonado (1533–1583), a highly regarded Jesuit biblical commentator.</note> adds this: *Christ is not speaking here philosophically and subtly, but popularly. ### BOOK II. MISCELLANIES

**The stars** <note>original Hebrew: *Hakkokavim*</note>, *namely the others.* For although it may seem to some that when the **greater lights** <note>A reference to Genesis 1:16, where the sun and moon are called the "two great lights."</note> are so named here, it should be referred to the quantity of their power and not to the extension of their mass; nevertheless, to one who diligently studies the text, it is clear that the Holy Spirit speaks here **by way of appearance** <note>original Greek: *doxastikos* (δοξαστικῶς), meaning according to common opinion or how things seem to the eyes.</note> and **popularly**, not **philosophically** <note>In this period, "philosophically" often meant "scientifically" or according to natural physics.</note>. > *The moon shines in a clear sky among the lesser stars,*
clearly following the opinion of the common people, who judge the Moon to be larger than the other stars because of its proximity to us. Therefore, **Lombard** <note>Peter Lombard, the medieval theologian mentioned on the previous page.</note> opposes the **Physicists** <note>Scientists of the natural world.</note> just as awkwardly as if someone were to attempt to refute Astronomers using the first chapter of **Moses** <note>The Book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note>.

XXIV. But if a universal statement presupposes divine revelation, it will be either a precept, a promise, a threat, or finally a simple assertion. For example, in **Matthew 23:2, 3**, the Savior says:
> *The Scribes and Pharisees sit on the seat of Moses; whatever they tell you, do it.*

# BOOK II. MISCELLANEOUS—

as *Abraham de Balmis*, a Jew, testifies: <note>Original Hebrew: יחיד אין לו משרת לפניו רק הוא משרת</note> "He is alone; he has no servant before him, but he himself serves." That is: it is so far from the case that this supposed and ignoble accent has royal ministers here, that it is rather itself a servant of others. 3. However, so that the use of the particle <note>Original Hebrew: עַד (*ad*, meaning "until" or "during")</note> may be more correctly established for us, and how we might investigate its meaning, it should be known that the particle <term>ad</term> is sometimes used by itself, and sometimes joined either with certain prefixes or with whole words. It is placed by itself in **Joshua 2:16**: *“Hide yourselves there* <note>Original Hebrew: עַד שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים (*ad sheloshet yamim*)</note> *for three days, until the pursuers return.”* Here, certainly, since the <term>Rebhia</term><note>A "disjunctive" accent that marks a pause in the verse.</note> accent had already preceded, no reason for a grammatical distinction is held in the <term>Jethib</term><note>A "disjunctive" accent that usually appears at the beginning of a word.</note> accent. Sometimes, however, it is joined with others and is marked by various accents without any distinction—namely <term>Jethib</term>, <term>Munach</term>, <term>Mahpach</term>, <term>Merca</term>, and <term>Teshir</term>.<note>These are technical names for Hebrew cantillation marks that indicate how the text is chanted and how words are grouped together.</note> For example, the particle <term>ad</term> merges with the following prefix <note>The Hebrew letter 'Shin' (שׁ) which acts as a relative pronoun "that" or "which."</note> as in **Song of Solomon 2:17**: <note>Original Hebrew: עַד שֶׁיָּפוּחַ הַיּוֹם (*ad she-yapuach ha-yom*)</note> *“until the day breathes,”* where the <term>Mahpach</term> accent occurs. In **Judges 5:7**: <note>Original Hebrew: חָדְלוּ עַד שַׁקַּמְתִּי (*chadlu ad shaqqamti*)</note> *“they ceased, until I arose,”* with the <term>Mahpach</term> accent. It is also joined with the word <note>Original Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר (*asher*, meaning "which" or "that")</note> in **Exodus 23:30**: *“little by little I will drive them out from before your face,* <note>Original Hebrew: עַד אֲשֶׁר תִּפְרֶה (*ad asher tiphreh*)</note> *until you become fruitful.”* In **Ruth 1:13**: *“would you [therefore stay...]”*

### VIII.

A doubt is also raised concerning the passage of the Prophet *Habakkuk 2:4*: "the righteous shall live by his faith" <note>Original Hebrew: וְצַדִּיק בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ יִחְיֶה (*ve-tzaddik be-emunato yihyeh*)</note>; *the just shall live by his faith.* For the phrase "by his faith" <note>Original Hebrew: בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ (*be-emunato*)</note> can be applied either to the subject—and is not, in fact, a material determination—or to the predicate, where it is taken formally: that is, it suggests the reason why the predicate is said of the subject. <note>In grammatical terms, the author is asking if "by faith" describes the *type* of person (the one who is just-by-faith) or the *manner* of their living (lives-by-faith).</note> The former sense is suggested by *Johannes Arnoldus Corvinus*, a <term>Remonstrant</term> <note>A follower of Jacobus Arminius; the Remonstrants were involved in a major 17th-century theological dispute over predestination and grace.</note>, in chapter 33 of his work against <term>Pierre Du Moulin</term> <note>A prominent Huguenot minister and theologian, often Latinized as Petrus Molinaeus.</note>, section 35. However, *Franciscus Junius* <note>A major 16th-century Reformed theologian known for his work on biblical interpretation.</note> follows this [interpretation] entirely in his *Parallels*, book 2, parallel 1, whose words I shall include here:

> *Perhaps the change we use in our method of interpretation will lead some to wonder; because the other interpretation is commonly accepted, in this manner: "the just shall live by faith," that is, in faith and through faith he shall obtain life. But, even if it is true that the just person, while he lives here, lives by faith, there are nevertheless two things that draw me toward the other interpretation. One is the logic of the argument itself, which is certainly far easier and clearer if you take it in this way rather than that. The other is the distinction within the Hebrew context, which I certainly cannot disregard. If we follow that distinction, it must be read entirely in this way: "He who is just by faith, shall live" <note>Original Greek: ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως, ζήσεται (*ho dikaios ek pisteōs, zēsetai*)</note>; and not, as is commonly read: "The just, shall live by faith" <note>Original Greek: ὁ δίκαιος, ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται (*ho dikaios, ek pisteōs zēsetai*)</note>.*

IX. However, even if both methods of punctuation <note>In this context, "punctuation" refers to how the sentence is structured and which words are grouped together for meaning.</note> are approved by some, it seems far different to me, partly from the Prophet himself, and partly from the citation in the New Testament. The Prophet contrasts two groups: those who are unwilling to wait for God’s promise and instead accuse Him of lying, and others who wait patiently until the Lord actually fulfills what He has promised. The destruction of the former is predicted, while for the latter, a life that will endure eternally. Just as those who are impatient of delay perish due to their distrust, so, on the contrary, those who wait patiently do not perish, but live **by their faith** <note>Original Hebrew: בֶּאֱמוּנָתָם (*be-emunatam*)</note>, because of that very faith which is inseparably connected to patience—or, as the Author of the *Epistle to the Hebrews 6:12* says, **through faith and patience** <note>Original Greek: διὰ πίστεως καὶ μακροθυμίας (*dia pisteos kai makrothymias*)</note>. 

And so, from the nature of this contrast, the cause of life is implied, just as on the other side distrust joined with impatience is the reason for destruction. Consequently, the phrase "by faith"—like other limiting terms—pertains to the predicate <note>The "predicate" is the part of the sentence that says something about the subject; here, it explains *how* the righteous person lives.</note>, and not at all to the subject. 

Furthermore, Saint Paul takes these same words in this sense in *Galatians 3:11*, as is clear from the argument he uses. For he says: *that no one is justified before God by the law is evident, because the righteous shall live by faith. But the law is not of faith.* The argument is such: he who

For some recognize a simple **Merca** <note>A Hebrew musical and grammatical accent that usually indicates a connection to the following word.</note> under the word **the righteous** <note>Original Hebrew: צדיק (*tsaddiq*)</note>; others, however, recognize a **Tiphcha** <note>A Hebrew accent that usually indicates a slight pause or separation.</note>. **Junius** <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a prominent Huguenot theologian and linguist.</note> did not observe this, and thus he insists so rigidly on the accents. **Secondly**, however, usually the **Soph-pasuk** <note>The vertical colon at the end of a Hebrew verse.</note> with **Silluk** <note>The principal accent on the last word of a verse.</note> has the "servant" accent **Merca** immediately before it and enjoys the neighboring "ruler" accent **Tiphcha**. Therefore, this punctuation <note>The author uses "accentuatio" to refer to the system of Hebrew cantillation marks which function as both musical notes and punctuation.</note> would be preferable and more likely true than that of Junius.

**Thirdly**, even if Junius's punctuation is strictly maintained, since the **Tiphcha** accent is not "regal" <note>In Hebrew grammar, accents are ranked as "emperors," "kings," "dukes," etc., to show how much of a pause they create. Thus in the same Prophet **Habakkuk 1:4**, we read: **perverted judgment goes forth** <note>Original Hebrew: יצא משפט מעקל (*yatsa mishpat me'uqqal*)</note>; here the words would be wrongly torn apart <note>Meaning, if you followed the accents too rigidly, you would break the connection between "judgment" and "perverted."</note>. Likewise in chapter **3:7**: **the curtains of the land of Midian trembled** <note>Original Hebrew: ירגזון יריעות ארץ מדין (*yirgazun yeri'ot erets midyan*)</note>. Here, the **construct state** <note>A Hebrew grammatical structure where two nouns are joined in a "belonging to" relationship—here, "curtains of the land."</note> does not allow the words to be separated. Add to this verse 11.

Elsewhere, such a limitation sometimes occupies the end of the proposition in this Prophet, as in verse 14, and sometimes the middle. Moreover, even if such a limitation were somewhat separated by a distinctive accent, the force of the text would still point in that direction, as in **Daniel 9:17**: **O Lord, cause your face to shine upon your sanctuary that is desolate, for the Lord's sake** <note>Original Hebrew: האר פניך על מקדשך השמם למען אדני (*ha'er paneyka al miqdashka hashamem lema'an adonay*)</note>. The ancient theologians wrote without vowel points and marks; they expressed their thoughts in pure and simple letters. *The Masoretes are their secular interpreters, mere grammarians; they have partially illuminated and partially obscured them with distinctions, accents, marks, and points, as interpreters are sometimes accustomed to do, being more devoted to their own imaginations and perceptions or more desirous of glory, so that they might seem to say something new, and to acquire fame for themselves by insulting the ancients—even though those ancients* (he refers here to the **Seventy Interpreters** <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, which many Christian scholars believed was divinely inspired.</note>) *shone with the illumination of the Holy Spirit.* For the *Masora* <note>original: Masoret</note> is nothing other than a *grammatical* tradition concerning *points, accents, syllables, words, and similar minutiae*: and in this it differs from the **Cabbala** <term>Kabbalah: the Jewish mystical and semiotic tradition that seeks hidden meanings in the text.</term>, in that the latter is indeed a tradition, but a *theological* one, concerning the more secret declaration of things and words.

...corrupted <note>original: "depravata"</note>, he thinks, and brings forward three examples: *Judges 19:3, Proverbs 31:6, and Jeremiah 2:24*, which the Illustrious **Sixtinus Amama** <note>1593–1629; a Dutch Reformed theologian and Hebrew scholar who defended the Masoretic text.</note> addressed in the cited place. **Gilbert Génébrard** <note>1535–1597; a French Benedictine and Hebraist.</note> had long ago produced other examples from *Psalm 2:6*, where "unto" <note>original: אל (el)</note> was substituted for "not" <note>original: לא (lo)</note>. *In his Commentary on Psalm 4:8*, he adds the passage *Nehemiah 2:13*, where he claims the **Masoretes** split into two words what had been joined into one: *I considered the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down* <note>original: אשר־הם פרוצים (asher-hem peruzim)</note>. **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>1089–1167; a celebrated Jewish polymath and biblical commentator.</note> thinks that here it should be read as "the broken ones" <note>original: המפרוצים (ha-meperuzim)</note>. He cites *Psalm 24:4*, where "his soul" <note>original: נפשו (nafsho)</note> is substituted for "my soul" <note>original: נפשי (nafshi)</note>; *Psalm 26:7*, where "to hear" <note>original: לשמוע (lishmoa)</note> occurs instead of "to listen" <note>original: לשמע</note>; and *Psalm 27:8*, where "seek ye" <note>original: בקשו (bikshu)</note> is read today instead of "seek me" <note>original: בקשני (bakasheni)</note>. The same author notes on *Psalm 78:47* that the Hebrew letter **Tav** <note>original: ת</note> bore the shape of a cross in other languages no less than in Hebrew; he claims that today, however, the shape has been changed by the wickedness of the Masoretes, so that the **mystery of the cross** <note>A common early modern Christian argument that the ancient Paleo-Hebrew letter Tav was shaped like a '+' or 'x', which they interpreted as a prophetic reference to Christ's crucifixion.</note> might be buried.

IV. Nor are there lacking those among the **Reformed** <note>Protestant scholars of the Reformation tradition.</note> who presume to pick at the **Masora** from time to time, whether this is done deliberately or because they do not know how else to avoid the force of certain arguments. **Joseph Justus Scaliger** <note>1540–1609; a titan of Renaissance scholarship known for his work in chronology and philology.</note> certainly, when he had contracted the words "throne of the Lord" <note>original: כס יה (kes yah)</note> in *Exodus 17:16* into a single word, "throne" <note>original: כסיה (kesyah)</note>, according to his own judgment—and indeed seeing that the Masora stood in his way—says thus in *Book 5 of On the Correction of Time, page 204*: *The critics of the Jews, whom they call Masoretes, read...*

the Catholics might wish, they cannot reject the <term>Masora</term> <note>The Masora is a traditional set of notes on the Hebrew Biblical text, compiled by Jewish scholars known as Masoretes between the 6th and 10th centuries to ensure the text was copied accurately.</note>. For if we look even only at the <term>Kethiv and Qere</term> <note>original: "כתיב & קרי"; these are technical terms for "what is written" in the text versus "what is read" in the margins when a scribal error or variation is noted.</note>, as they call them, the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible used by the Roman Catholic Church.</note> agrees perfectly with the <term>Masoretes</term> in the following places; specifically where it followed the authority of the original sources rather than the Greek text.

For example, they noted in *Joshua 15:47* that instead of "the sea the border" <note>original: הַיָּם הַגְּבוּל</note>, one should read "the Great Sea" <note>original: הַיָּם הַגָּדוֹל, *mare magnum*</note>, which is what the Vulgate agrees with. Furthermore, even if a word has happened to fall out of the <term>Authentic text</term> <note>The original Hebrew source text.</note> and was supplied by the care of the Masoretes, the Vulgate agrees there as well. This can be seen in *2 Samuel 8:3* where the word "Euphrates" <note>original: פְרָת</note> is added; in *2 Kings 19:31* where the word "of hosts" <note>original: צְבָאוֹת</note> is supplied; and in *Jeremiah 31:38* with the plural participle "coming" <note>original: בָּאִים</note>.

The same reasoning applies if even a single letter is missing, as in *1 Samuel 17:23*. There, the word "from the caves" <note>original: מִמַּעַרְוֹת</note> is translated as "from the camps," indicating that the genuine reading is "from the ranks" <note>original: מִמַּעַרְכֹוֹת</note>, exactly as it was emended in the Masora. Therefore, let the Masora hold at least some authority even among the Catholics; for it will thereafter be easy to conclude that the Masoretes [acted] with the same faith and industry...

...will confirm this? Who will rashly believe one who makes such claims? For often a diminished **Vav** <note>The sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ו). In manuscript tradition, letters were sometimes written smaller than usual for specific scribal reasons.</note> occurs without any connotation of nails <note>The author is likely referring to the "pierced hands and feet" in Psalm 22, which is associated with the nails of the crucifixion.</note> or any hidden mystery. The Catholics assert that in the **Vulgate** version of **Psalm 22**, a **Vav** was changed into a **Jod** <note>The smallest Hebrew letter (י).</note> by a scribal error; but did a scribal error really give birth to a mystery? Such things are twisted into "mysteries" by accident, rather than being the aim of the original author’s intention. This is clearly evident from these two points:

1. From the same **Psalm** cited by Folanus <note>Likely referring to a contemporary commentator or scholar.</note>, in verse 19, the <term>Kethiv</term> <note>The word as it is written in the main body of the Hebrew text.</note> has *aniyyim* <note>original: עניים; "the poor" or "afflicted."</note>, while the <term>Qere</term> <note>The word as it is traditionally read or corrected in the margin.</note> has *anavim* <note>original: ענוים; "the humble" or "meek."</note>. But should we truly believe it was the mind of the **Holy Spirit** that the hope of the humble will not perish only if they are also poor, afflicted, and needy? Shall we then exclude the wealthy, and those for whom everything is supplied in abundance and succeeds according to their heart's desire, from that expectation or hope—provided all other things are equal?

Next, how often, I ask, are **lo** (not) and **lo** (to him) <note>original: לֹא & לּוֹ. These words sound the same in Hebrew but have opposite meanings: "not" versus "to him/it."</note> interchanged with one another, even though they are particles with contradictory meanings? It is impossible for God to present us with such diverse—indeed, entirely opposite—meanings within one and the same context. 

Finally, to add this as well: where the [vowel] points are entirely missing, as in **Jeremiah 51:3**, and a word is redundant, what sort of mystery do you judge to be hidden there?

X. Away, then, with those mystical interpretations—or rather, fabrications—which are utterly foreign to the intention of the **Holy Spirit**. Indeed, if everyone were eager to produce and assert such things at their own whim, we would eventually descend into fictions similar to those of the **Talmudists** <note>Scholars and followers of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>. For it is customary for them to read the authentic text in various ways, provided they can extract from it whatever happens to please them. See **Capellus** <note>Louis Cappel (1585–1658), a famous Protestant scholar of Hebrew who argued that the vowel points in the Hebrew Bible were not original.</note>, whom I mentioned above, on page 42; and **Maimonides** <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> in *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Nevochim*</note> on page 473, who believes that such various Rabbinic readings should be accepted under the guise of allegories.

If we wish to observe what is approved by the learned, it appears that the <term>Masora</term> <note>The body of traditional notes on the form of the Hebrew biblical text, used to ensure its accurate transmission.</note> originated from the **Prophets** themselves—at least those who appeared in a later age—and thus it might be doubted whether it is proper for anyone to depart from these types of marginal notes. We are absolutely bound to embrace the opinions and decrees of the **Prophets** as divine, provided it is clear what they are and that they should indeed be credited to the **Prophets**. Yet the **Masora** does not contain just a few observations, but a great many, some of which were even fashioned in centuries far removed from the memory of the **Prophets**. Nor is it easy, even with the greatest sharp-mindedness, to [discern] an infalli-

...which reading could be placed in the text, just as double accents are placed in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments; the author refers to the two different systems of musical accents (cantillation) used for reading Exodus 20.</note>, *Exodus 20*. However, the reading which seemed more probable to the <term>Masoretes</term> <note>The medieval Jewish scholars who standardized the Hebrew Bible's text and punctuation.</note>, they chose to present through the vowel points in the text and through the letters in the margin. They did not prescribe anything to limit our freedom in such ambiguous cases, especially if we wish to embrace another reading that is more likely and which the <term>Ketiv</term> <note>original: כתיב; the "written" Hebrew consonants in the main body of the text.</note> provides.

It cannot be denied that this has been observed by Christian interpreters. Hence, our *Blessed Luther*, when he believed he could more rightly attain the mind of the divine writer by preserving the <term>Ketiv</term>, adhered to it alone and bid the <term>Qere</term> <note>original: קרי; the "read" version suggested by the marginal notes.</note> to be gone. For example, in *Jeremiah 2:20*, it said "I will not pass over" <note>original: לא אעבור (*lo e’evor*)</note> in the margin; but Luther, following the text, read "I will not serve" <note>original: לא אעבוד (*lo e’evod*)</note>, which he translated as: *I will not be so subject* <note>original German: "Ich will nicht ſo unterworffen ſeyn."</note>. Luther, according to the reading of the text, translates: *one wishes* <note>original German: "man wünſchet."</note>. In *Daniel 9:24*, the text has "to seal up" <note>original: לחתם (*lachatêm*)</note> as if it should be read "to seal" <note>original: לחתום (*lachtom*)</note>, just as Luther also rendered it: *that sin be sealed up* <note>original German: "daß die Sün-de zugeſiegelt werde."</note>; but the Masoretes noted in the margin that it should be read "to finish or consume" <note>original: להתם (*lehatêm*)</note>. In *Joshua 8:12*, the <term>Ketiv</term> has "waters for the city" <note>original: מים לעיר (*mayim la-ir*)</note>. Luther translates this as: *towards evening* <note>original German: "gegen Abendwerts"; this likely refers to a variation between the Hebrew words for 'sea/west' and 'water'.</note>.

XII. This is the authority of the <term>Masorah</term> <note>The body of Jewish tradition and notes used to preserve the exact text of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, which *Génébrard* <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine scholar and critic of the Masoretic points.</note> attempts to diminish through the examples brought forward in section 3. Therefore, it would have had to be said: "I will declare the decree of God" <note>original Hebrew: אֲסַפְּרָה חֹק אֵל (*asappera choq el*)</note>; but the word "to/God" <note>original: אֵל (*el*)</note> could not and should not have been placed before the other word, as *Génébrard* thinks. *Bellarmine* <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), an influential Jesuit Cardinal.</note>, *Galatino* <note>Pietro Galatino (1460–1540), a Franciscan Hebraist.</note>, and others make a similar error, to whom *Isaiah 53:4*—"smitten by God" <note>original Hebrew: מֻכֵּה אֱלֹהִים (*mukkeh Elohim*)</note>—sounds like "a smitten God." They observe neither the **construct state** nor the well-worn Hebrew rule which dictates that a noun joined to an adjective must precede it. *Joannes Alba* <note>Juan de Silva, a Spanish Jesuit scholar.</note> also stumbles by failing to observe the construct state when he translates the words in *Haggai 2:8*—"the desire of the nations shall come" <note>original Hebrew: בָּאוּ חֶמְדַּת גּוֹיִם (*ba'u chemdat goyim*)</note>—as...

### CHAPTER VI.

...to which you would prefer to grant your agreement; for it is not a fatal error to prefer the <term>Kethiv</term> <note>original Hebrew: כתיב; the "written" form of the biblical text as it appears on the parchment, which sometimes differs from the traditionally spoken version.</note>, provided that it better aligns with the intention of the writer. Although in this case, all other factors find their place: for the word "what" <note>original Hebrew: מה (*mah*)</note> fits the text most aptly when separated, and far more correctly than if you were to join it with the following word, as if the letter *Mem* <note>original Hebrew: מ</note> were a prefix—specifically the *Mem* used as a grammatical marker for a participle. 

Whatever the case may be, the "mystery" that **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>A celebrated 12th-century Spanish rabbi, philosopher, and biblical commentator.</note> hints at here is not insisted upon by the **Masoretes** <note>The medieval Jewish scholars who standardized the Hebrew Bible's text and pronunciation.</note>; thus they did not divide the words themselves because of some hidden mystery, just as they did not in *Job 38 and 40*. If any such mystery is emphasized here, it should be considered an addition by other Rabbis rather than the original intent of the Masoretic scholars.

Similarly, when it is said in *Psalm 24:3–4*: *"Who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart,"* **who has not lifted up my soul unto vanity** <note>original Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר לֹא נָשָׂא לַשָּׁוְא נַפְשִׁי (*asher lo nasa l’shav napshi*)</note>—that is, *who has not taken my soul in vain*—the Masoretes do not prescribe the reading to us even in the slightest. Instead, it remains open to anyone to embrace that reading which he judges to be truer. 

In my judgment, however, the reading that exists in the written text is truer because of its cohesion with the surrounding words. For it would be poorly said by **David**: *"Who shall stand in the place of his holiness?"* (namely, the Lord's) if there were then added: *"he who does not take up **my soul** <note>original Hebrew: נפשי (*napshi*)</note> in vain."* Such a shift in perspective would be awkward, regardless of how one might try to explain the meaning of the phrase.

...interpreter: *“Call now, if there is anyone who will answer you; and turn to one of the saints.”* <note>original: *voca ergo, si est, qui tibi respondeat & ad aliquem sanctorum convertere* — This is a translation of Job 5:1.</note> From this, the **Catholic proponents** derive the **Invocation of the Saints**, <term>Invocation of the Saints: the practice of asking deceased holy people to intercede with God, a point of major contention during the Reformation.</term> while they interpret the particles *“to whom”* <note>original: אל מי (*el mi*)</note> as *“to someone,”* contrary to what the nature of the language requires and common usage dictates. **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation.</note> defends this version so strictly in *Book 2 on the Word of God, Chapter XII*, that he writes that **Chemnitz** <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a leading Lutheran theologian known as the "Second Martin" for his role in consolidating the Reformation.</note> was "drunk" when he criticized the **Vulgate** <note>The Latin Bible translation authorized by the Catholic Church.</note> version in this passage. However, the matter stands far differently if we consult the **Masorah**. <note>The Masorah is a traditional system of marginal notes used by Jewish scholars to ensure the precise transmission of the Hebrew Bible text.</note> Let us know, therefore, that the Masorah noted that those small words, *“to whom,”* <note>original: אל מי (*el mi*)</note> occur three times, and with the prefix, *“and to whom,”* <note>original: ואל מי (*ve-el mi*)</note> four times, and never without an interrogative sense <note>That is, these words are always used to ask a question (To whom?), never as an indefinite pronoun (to someone).</note>. **Isaiah 40:18:** *And to whom will you liken God?* <note>original: ואל מי (*ve-el mi*)</note>
**In the same chapter, verse 25:** *And to whom will you liken me, that I should be his equal? says the Holy One.* <note>original: ואל מי (*ve-el mi*)</note>
**2 Kings 9:5:** *The young man said: “A word for you, O Prince.” And Jehu said: “To whom of all of us?” And he said: “To you, O Prince.”* <note>original: אל מי (*el mi*)</note>
**Ezekiel 31:2:** *To whom are you made like in your greatness?* <note>original: אל מי (*el mi*)</note>
**In the same chapter, verse 18:** *To whom are you likened?* <note>original: אל מי (*el mi*)</note>

### III. In order to correctly understand this phrasing and to resolve this difficulty, it should be noted both what the Hebrew word *shebi* <term>shebi (שבי): a Hebrew term for a body of captives or the state of captivity</term> means, and the logic of the contrast between these Hebrew phrases: *he led captivity captive* <note>original Latin: "shaba shebi" (שבה שבי) or "shaba shebiyah" (שבה שביה)</note> and *he returned the captivity* <note>original Latin: "shub shebi" (שוב שבי) or "heshib shebiyah" (השיב שביה)</note>. Indeed, the enemies and the captives themselves are called *shebi* <note>שבי</note>, as is clear from **Nehemiah 1:3** and **Numbers 31:12**. Therefore, from the fact that "captives of the enemy" are understood by the term *shebi*, one may argue against the **Catholics** <term>Pontificios: a term used by the author to refer to Roman Catholic theologians</term> as follows: Those who are not enemies of Christ, he did not lead away with him as captives into heaven. But those whom the Catholics claim were enclosed in **Limbo** <term>Limbo: specifically the *Limbus Patrum*, the place where the souls of the Old Testament saints were thought to wait for Christ</term> are not enemies of Christ. Therefore, he did not lead them into heaven as captives.

### IV. Now we must weigh how the phrases mentioned above relate to one another. There are some who contend that the *former* phrase can be understood in two ways: 1. *Passively*: "he led captivity captive," that is, he led a crowd of captives. 2. *Actively*: "he led captivity captive," that is, he led those who were the captors themselves, or those who previously held others captive. But the formal meaning of these words, when joined in this manner, supports only the first interpretation; and it happens only by coincidence that the "captor" is led captive—that is, the one who already holds others as captives. ### BOOK II. MISCELLANIES

Therefore, the phrase should not be judged based on such an accidental perspective, as it does not rely on proven examples. For "to take captive those who take captive"—that is, those who have already imprisoned others—is not expressed by the Hebrews as *shaba shebi* <note>original Hebrew: שבה שבי</note>, but rather as *shaba le-shobim* <note>original Hebrew: שבה לשובים</note> as seen in **Isaiah 14:2**, or *lakach shebi gibbor* <note>original Hebrew: לקח שבי גבור</note>, which means "he wrested the captives from the mighty," as in **Isaiah 49:25** (and likewise in **Luke 11:22**). 

As is therefore evident, it is not from the nature of the Hebrew language itself that "to take captivity [captive]" means to imprison the captors who hold others captive, nor does it mean to make captives anew of those who were already held as captives by others. Indeed, even **Cornelius à Lapide** <note>A prominent Jesuit biblical commentator (1567–1637) whose work was a standard reference in the 17th century.</note> cannot deny this latter point in his *Commentary on Hebrews, chapter 4*. Therefore, that opinion remains sound and unshaken which attributes such peculiar meanings to the specific circumstances of the person captured, rather than to the phrase itself.

### V.
But now we must deal with examples. Let us take these examples of the first phrase: In **Numbers 21:1**, *Arad, the Canaanite king*, fought with the Israelites, *and took some of them captive* <note>original Hebrew: וישב ממנו שבי (va-yisheb mimmenu shebi)</note>. In **2 Chronicles 28:17** <note>original Latin: 2. Paral. XXVIII, 17. "Paralipomenon" is the Greek-derived name for the Books of Chronicles.</note>, *the Edomites came and attacked the Judeans and carried away captives* <note>original Hebrew: וישבו שבי (va-yisbu shebi)</note>, which had been described in verse 8 as *and they took many captives* <note>original Hebrew: וישבו שביה גדולה (va-yisbu shebiyah gedolah)</note>. By contrast, however, the phrase *shub shebit* <note>original Hebrew: שבות שבית</note> or *heshib shibah* <note>original Hebrew: הישיב שיבה</note> means to release or undo the captivity.

### BOOK II. CHAPTER VIII.

->On the origin and variety of Proper Names,<-
->and what must be most carefully<-

I. Authors disagree as to where the proper names of the **Sacred Text** <note>The Bible/Scripture.</note> sometimes originate, and by what specific reasoning the explanation might match the words of Scripture itself, which seem to stand in place of a derivation <note>A linguistic explanation of a word's origin.</note>. We read in 1 Samuel 1:20: *Hannah conceived and bore a son, and called his name* **Samuel** <note>Hebrew: שמואל (*Shemu’el*)</note> — *because I have asked him of the Lord* <note>Hebrew: כי מיהוה שאלתיו (*Ki me-Yehovah she'altiv*)</note>. # JEWISH CABBALA
## A BRIEF EXPLANATION.
### I.

There is a very well-known saying of the Jews concerning the sacred writings: *In the Torah, there is not a single letter on which great mountains do not hang* <note>original Hebrew: בתורה : אין לך אות אחת שאין הרים גדולים תלויים בה</note>; *that is, there is not one letter in the Law upon which great mountains do not hang.* <note>original Latin: "non est in Lege una litera, a qua non magni dependeant montes"</note> They extend this principle even to the <term>apices</term> <note>The "crowns" (tagin) or decorative flourishes added to the tops of certain Hebrew letters by scribes.</note> with which the letters are marked on top, which resemble sharp thorns. Some scholars relate this to the words of our Savior in **Matthew 5:18**: *not one iota, nor one <term>tittle</term> <note>original Greek: κεραία (keraia); literally a "little horn," referring to the smallest stroke or hook used to distinguish one letter from another.</note> shall pass from the law, until all things are accomplished.* 

Albeit this might be considered a hyperbolic statement, it is suggested as such even by those passages where only the vowel points <note>The "nikkud" or dots used in Hebrew to represent vowels, which were added to the consonant-only text in later centuries.</note> remain, while all the actual letters have been obliterated by the damage of time. For example, in **Judges 20:13**, where only the points for *sons* <note>Hebrew: בני (Bnei)</note> appear; in **Ruth 1:17**, where only those for *to me* <note>Hebrew: אלי (Eli)</note> appear; in **2 Samuel 16:23**, where only those for *man* <note>Hebrew: איש (Ish)</note> appear; in **2 Kings 19:37**, where only those for *his sons* <note>Hebrew: בניו (Banaiv)</note> appear; or in **Jeremiah 31:38**, where the vowel points for *coming* <note>Hebrew: באם (Ba’im)</note> are to be read. This is also evident when even a single <term>Jota</term> <note>The "Yod," the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note> has been lost, as seen in **1 Samuel 20:2** <note>Hebrew: יעשה (Ya’aseh)</note>, **2 Samuel 22:8** <note>Hebrew: ויגעש (Wayiga’ash)</note>, and **Nehemiah 12:46** <note>Hebrew: ראש (Rosh)</note>, as the examination of these cited passages themselves demonstrates.

### IV.

XVI. Likewise, there is another method called <term>Sofei Tevot</term>. Its rule is this: when the words of a phrase, ending in various letters, produce a new word, a mystical meaning is indicated. In the **Atbash** <note>original: "Athbasch"; a substitution cipher where the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, etc.</note> alphabet, the reader leaves one letter and substitutes another in the writing which is at its side; in this particular place, he writes a **Yod** (י) for a **Mem** (מ) which is near it, a **Tet** (ט) for a **Gimel** (ג), and an **Aleph** (א) for a **Tav** (ת). And so it goes with the rest, until that entire sentence is completed. Clearly, therefore, **Daniel** was no less devoted to this **Cabbala** <term>Cabbala: Jewish mystical tradition that often uses linguistic ciphers to find hidden divine truths.</term> than **Jeremiah**.

XXIII. Nor do they claim that such things were hidden from **Isaiah**. Whence **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> comments as follows: *It is possible to interpret Tabeel* <note>original: טבאל</note> *as one who is "not good" in the eyes of the **Place** <note>original: מקום (Ha-Makom, "The Place"), a common Rabbinic title for God</note>; and furthermore, according to a specific type of **Gematria** <term>Gematria: Usually a numerical system, but here used broadly to describe the "Albam" letter-substitution cipher.</term> called **Albam** <note>original: אלב"ם; a cipher where the first letter (Aleph) is swapped with the twelfth (Lamed), and the second (Bet) with the thirteenth (Mem).</note>, if you swap the letters **T-B** <note>Tet and Bet</note> for **R-M** <note>Resh and Mem</note> and the letter **L** <note>Lamed</note> for **Sh** <note>Shin</note>, the "Son of Tabeal" becomes the **Son of Remaliah**.* In this way, the Prophet wished to hide the proper name, so that he might not perhaps offend the King. It should be noted that **Kimchi**, in his *Book of Roots* <note>Rabbi David Kimchi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, a premiere Hebrew grammarian and commentator.</note>, relates the following: *The border by which you shall inherit the land* <note>original: גְּבוּל אֲשֶׁר תִּתְנַחֲלוּ אֶת־הָאָרֶץ</note> *is just like "this"* <note>original: כְּמוֹ זֶה</note>; *and likewise, Jonathan* <note>Targum Jonathan, the ancient Aramaic translation of the Prophets.</note> *also renders it as "this" [in Aramaic]* <note>original: דֵּין (dein)</note>; *and indeed, the letter **Gimel** (ג) corresponds to the letter **Zayin** (ז) in the **Atbach** alphabet.*

In the **Atbach** <term>Atbach: A substitution cipher where letters are paired based on their numerical values summing to 10, 100, or 1000. Here, Gimel (3) and Zayin (7) are paired because they sum to 10.</term> alphabet, **Gimel** answers to the letter **Zayin**. **Schindler** <note>Valentin Schindler (died 1604), a Lutheran philologist and author of a famous five-language lexicon.</note> also agrees with **Kimchi** in his *Lexicon*.

The same Rabbi [Kimchi], in that same work, when treating the passage in **Ezekiel 21:15** <note>In many English bibles, this is Ezekiel 21:20.</note> where the phrase *the point of the sword* <note>original: אִבְחַת חֶרֶב (ivchat cherev)</note> appears, speaks thus: *There are those who interpret **Ivchat** (אבחת) as if it were written **Tivchat** (טבחת) [meaning "slaughter"], by the mutual exchange of the letters **Aleph** (א) and **Tet** (ט) according to the **Atbach** alphabet.* Let **Schindler** be consulted again on this point, for he also draws the **Chaldean** <note>Aramaic</note> language into the fellowship of this **Cabbala**.

The composition of Cabbalistic methods.

XXV. Nor indeed do these simple methods alone prevail; for here and there, composite methods also occur. The Jews hold **circumcision** in high regard, as is clear from the words of the **Baal Ha-Turim** <note>Jacob ben Asher (c. 1269–1343), a legal authority whose commentary on the Torah is famous for using word-codes and numerical proofs.</note> on chapter XI of the book of **Numbers**: *Circumcision delivers one from the judgment or the punishment of **Gehenna** <note>Hell</note> or the infernal regions.*

They confirm this dogma through the **Cabbala**, but of the composite kind, using **Deuteronomy 30:12**: *Who shall go up for us to heaven?* <note>original: המכוֹת הַעֹלֹת לָנוּ בַּשָּׁמַיִם הִיא; The author appears to be leading into a proof where the first letters of these words spell "Milah" (Circumcision) and the last letters spell the name of God.</note>

...to say: *Who shall go up for us to heaven?* <note>A quote from Deuteronomy 30:12.</note> The first letters [spell] **Milah** <note>original: מילה (circumcision)</note> and the final letters [spell] **Yahweh** <note>The Tetragrammaton or Divine Name.</note>, to say that one cannot ascend to the Name [God] unless he is circumcised; and likewise: *Walk before me and be perfect* <note>Genesis 17:1</note>, which is said concerning circumcision.

For if you join the final letters with the first letters of the words *Israel who come* <note>original: ישראל הבאים (Yisrael Ha-ba'im)</note>, it produces **Milah**, that is, circumcision. For example, the 3rd letter (Gimel) and 7th letter (Zayin) are swapped because 3+7=10.</term>. Valentin Schindler <note>A 16th-century Lutheran hebraist.</note> also agrees with Kimchi in his *Lexicon*. That is, there are those who interpret *Ibchat* as if it were written *Tibchat* <note>original: טִבְחַת (slaughtering/slaying)</note>, with the letters **Aleph** & **Tet** and **Bet** & **Het** being swapped for one another from the Atbach Alphabet. One may again consult Schindler, who also draws the Aramaic [Chaldean] language into the company of this Cabbalistic method.

<note>This Hebrew passage is summarized and explained in the Latin text that follows.</note> This is to say: *Who shall go up for us to heaven?* <note>Deuteronomy 30:12</note>. What indeed do they gather from this? They answer:* **To tell you that for the sake of the Sabbath and Circumcision, the Israelites were redeemed from Egypt.** <note>original Latin: "ut dicat Mosi tibi, quod Israëlitae liberati sunt à servitute Ægyptiaca, ob..."</note>

XXVI. In this way, indeed, acrostics and words are joined, but in other cases, a special combination is also found. *In Genesis 11:29, Moses says: "Abraham and Nahor took wives: the name of Abram’s wife was Sarai; the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah," as the Vulgate version has it.* Scholars disagree on who that **Iscah** <note>Hebrew: יסכה</note> might be. XXXII. Many more examples occur here and there: but because these things are not well known to the general public, it is better to add something about the general rules than to break off the discussion. Thus, the tips of the letters are called <term>tagin</term> <note>original: חגין (*chagin*), likely a scribal variant for תגין (*tagin*)</note>, <term>zinin</term> <note>original: זינין</note>, or <term>ketarim</term> <note>original: כתרים</note>. The word *ketarim* means **crowns**, and they acquired this name because they adorn the top of the letters where several strokes meet, just like a crown. They are called *zinin* because they **resemble little spikes**. They likewise interpret the word *kotz* <note>original: קוץ, literally "thorn"</note> as "crowns," following the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> and Arabic. For in Arabic, *taj* <note>original: تاج</note> is a **diadem**, and *tawwaja* <note>original: توج</note> means **he crowned**. Capellus <note>Louis Cappel (1585–1658), a French Protestant scholar of the Hebrew Bible</note> asserts that they are also designated as *kotzim* <note>spikes or thorns</note>, though this is contested by Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a celebrated Hebraist</note> on the last page of his *Treatise on the Antiquity of Points*, contrary to what was done in his *Talmudic Lexicon*. They make God Himself the author of these crowns, as is found in the *Beth Israel* <note>House of Israel</note>, page 166, column 2. These words are cited in the aforementioned Lexicon under the entry *kotz*, where the Jews say that God looked ahead to Rabbi Akiva ben Joseph <note>A central figure in Judaism and the development of the Mishnah, legendary for his ability to derive mountains of laws from the smallest marks on the Torah</note>, whose Alphabet I have also found; and because it is rare, I shall include it here.

<header>JUDAICA</header>

Seven letters require three tips <term>apices</term>; namely, the letters *Shin, Ayin, Tet, Nun, Zayin, Gimmel,* and *Tsadi* <note>represented by the mnemonic acronym שעטנז גץ (Sha'atnez Getz)</note>, as you also find in *Galatinus*, book 2, chapter 14, *On the Secrets of Catholic Truth* <note>original: *de Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis*</note>, where *Abraham Pici* clarifies the matter with an example. To be sure, authors vary, and I recently brought forward a double example from the *Baal ha-Turim* <note>A significant 14th-century biblical commentary by Jacob ben Asher</note> where, according to the Alphabet of Rabbi Akiva, the letter *He* (ה) has five tips, and the *Qof* (ק) has three. In Synagogues, the Mosaic scroll <term>codex Mosaicus</term> <note>The handwritten Torah scroll used in worship</note> is devoid of points <note>referring to the *niqqud* or vowel markings</note>; hence, these tips are used in certain places in their stead, in greater or lesser numbers, to designate mystical secrets along with other small non-vocalic points. However, since the scribes are cautioned not to paint the tips too thickly, but rather in the manner of a very thin thread resembling hair, no artist has been so successful that his craft could fully express that subtlety. Consequently, in printed works today, not even a shadow of that marking remains. Similarly, the sign for softening a letter—the small line known as the *Raphe* <note>A horizontal bar used in Hebrew grammar to indicate a soft, non-plosive pronunciation</note>—has also been removed, and traces of it are not seen except in the texts of Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5.

<header>CABBALA <note>The Kabbalah; Jewish mystical tradition</note></header>

Indeed, they desire that the Kabbalah depend upon faith. Yet, here is what you should hold according to the opinion of those Kabbalists: The letter *Beth* <note>The second letter of the Hebrew alphabet: ב</note> has two tips <term>apices</term>, *referring to the dual court, the upper and the lower: the divine and the human* <note>original Hebrew: כנגד בית דין של מעלה ושל מטה</note>. The *Vav* <note>The sixth letter: ו</note> has a single tip, because on the sixth day (which the *Vav* denotes as a numeral) the first man was created, *the unique governor of the lower world* <note>original Hebrew: יחיד בעולם ומתחתיו</note>. The *Zayin* <note>The seventh letter, here written as 'Dſain': ז</note> has three, because on the seventh day (which the *Zayin* signifies in numbers), where rest was commanded, man ought to delight himself with three pleasures: *food, drink, and clean garments* <note>original Hebrew: מאכל משתה וכסות נקיה</note>; and so it goes for the others. The *Pe* <note>The seventeenth letter: פ</note>, however, is bent more than is normal, apart from its tips, *to warn you that prayers in which a broken and contrite heart and a bowed spirit are not joined, are not pleasing to God* <note>original Hebrew: לומר לכל תפלה שאין בה לב נשבר ונדכה ורוח כפוף חינם היא; this alludes to the humility required in prayer, referencing Psalm 51</note>.

The Masorah <note>The tradition of scribal notes that ensure the correct transmission of the Hebrew Bible</note> notes two things: 1. *It does not occur elsewhere in full form* <note>original: לית מלא בתורה</note>, that is, it is no longer found written with a double *Jod* <note>The Hebrew letter י</note> in the Law [the Torah]. 2. *A point is placed over the latter Jod* <note>original: נקוד על יוד בתרא</note>. *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> provides this reason for that extraordinary point:

*Whenever the word "beinecha" <note>"between you"; ביניך</note> occurs in the Scriptures, it is written "defectively" <term>deficiently</term> <note>meaning without the extra letter Jod</note>; but in this place, it is "full" <term>plene</term>. Therefore, read it as: "May the Lord judge between me and you [Abraham]" <note>original: וביניֹך</note>, and [judge] your son (O Hagar, who has become arrogant—for the Jod implies a suffix). This is because Sarah cast an "evil eye" on Hagar’s fetus, which caused her to suffer a miscarriage. This is the very thing the Angel says to Hagar in verse 11: "Behold, you are going to be pregnant." But had she not already conceived in verse 4? What need was there to announce it as if it were something new? Thus, it teaches that the first fetus had already been cast out from the womb by a miscarriage, for which Sarah was the cause; this is what is suggested by the superfluous and dotted Jod.* <note>The commentator is explaining the mystical-linguistic reason for a "typo" in the divine text, suggesting the extra letter refers to the child Hagar lost before Ishmael was born.</note>

<margin>
On numbering [words] in a single text.
</margin>
...method, division, writing, and reading. Numbering is of two kinds: it looks either at words within the same text, following each other in their proper order; or at words from different texts, regardless of where they are taken from. We have an example of the first kind in *Exodus 1:7*. It is said there: *the sons of Israel fructified* <note>original: פָּרוּ (*paru*)</note>, *and increased themselves* <note>original: וַיִּשְׁרְצוּ (*vayishretzu*)</note>, *and grew* <note>original: וַיִּרְבּוּ (*vayirbu*)</note>, *and were multiplied* <note>original: וַיַּעַצְמוּ (*vaya'atzmu*)</note>, *and were strengthened* <note>original: בִּמְאֹד (*bim’od*)</note>, *exceedingly* <note>original: מְאֹד (*me’od*)</note>, *exceedingly*. This is the observation: *there are six words here* <note>original: שִׁשָּׁה לִבּוֹת הֵן (*shishah libbot hen*)</note> *corresponding to women giving birth in one womb* <note>original: כְּנֶגֶד יוֹלְדוֹת בְּכֶרֶס אֶחָד (*k'neged yoldot b'cheres echad*)</note>; that is, there are six terms used here referring to the Israelite women, who brought forth six children from a single conception while they still lived in Egypt <note>This is a famous Midrashic interpretation explaining the rapid population growth of the Israelites</note>. Whether what they indicate here is absurd can be seen in Aristotle’s *History of Animals*, Book 7, Chapter 4; Pererius in his *Commentary on Exodus*; and Doctor Calixtus in his *Disputation on the First Twenty Chapters of Exodus*. Bernegger, in the *Fragments* prefixed to Justin, cites these words from Pliny: *Trogus is the authority that in Egypt, seven are born from one womb at the same time.*

<margin>
In different texts.
</margin>
XXXIIX. In the second kind, the *Baal Ha-Turim* <note>Jacob ben Asher (c. 1269–1343), a famous biblical commentator known for his mystical word-counts and connections</note> is most extensive throughout all the books of Moses. For example, in *Genesis 1:2*: *and the earth was "tohu"* <note>formless/chaos; original: תֹהוּ</note>. His note is as follows: *The numerical value is 412, and it returns in a cycle to the destruction [of the Temple]; for behold, "tohu" [equals 412]. This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw the destruction of the Temple at the creation of the world.* <note>original: תסו"ב הכל וחוזר חלילות לת חרבן והנה תהו . מלמד שצפה הקב"ה בבריאת העולם בחרבן הבית. The word "Tohu" (תֹהוּ) has a numerical value of 411; adding 1 for the word itself—a common practice in Gematria—reaches 412, which the author connects to the Temple's ruin.</note>

<header># JEWISH STUDIES</header>

It was destroyed in the year of "void" <note>Hebrew: *Tohu* (תהו)</note> which stood for 400 years and was destroyed in the year 411. The Second Temple <note>The "Second House"</note> stood according to the count of the word "she was" <note>Hebrew: *Hayetah* (היתה)</note> and afterwards "darkness" <note>Hebrew: *Choshech* (חשך)</note> hints at the exile.

The meaning is: the word *void* <note>original: תהו (*tohu*)</note> occurs twice in the Holy Scripture (namely, joined with *and emptiness* <note>original: ובהו (*v'bohu*)</note>). For so it must be explained from the intercolumnar Masora <note>The *Masora* are traditional scribal notes on the Hebrew Bible text; "intercolumnar" refers to notes written between the columns of a scroll</note>, which this author mostly refers to in this matter. Now the Masora has "2 in the text" <note>original: ב' 'דס</note>, fully written as "two are joined" <note>original: דסמיכין ב' (*d'smichin bet*)</note>, that is, two words are connected in this way, or they appear together twice (*void* & *and emptiness*) in this place—specifically in Genesis 1:2 and Jeremiah 4:23: *I saw the earth, and behold, it was void* <note>original: תהו (*tohu*)</note>. 

This comparison teaches mystically that the author <note>identified as "S. B."</note> saw in the very creation of the world the destruction of Solomon's Temple: for it was devastated in the year 411, which lies hidden in the word *void* <note>Hebrew letters function as numbers: Tav (400) + He (5) + Vav (6) = 411</note> by reason of its numerical value. For it stood for 410 years and was destroyed in the year 411. 

But the Second Temple lasted 420 years, according to the number produced by the word *she was* <note>original: היתה (*hayetah*); He (5) + Yod (10) + Tav (400) + He (5) = 420</note>. Afterwards in the text of the Mosaic history <note>The Torah/Pentateuch</note> follows *darkness* <note>original: חשך (*choshech*)</note>, which denotes the exiles of the Jews. We find such things in that author—not three hundred or six hundred instances, but almost infinite.

<margin>On the inversion of letters</margin>
XL. Nor is it far from our purpose to note that the **Kabbalists** <note>Practitioners of Jewish mysticism</note> retain the same words but transpose their letters with such ingenuity that a suitable meaning emerges. For example, in Genesis 28:5 and 25:20, Laban is called **the Aramean** <note>original: הָאֲרַמִּי (*Ha-Arami*)</note>, which is to say, the Syrian; but the Teachers <note>The Rabbis or Jewish commentators</note> pointedly transform this into **the Deceiver** <note>original: הָרַמַּאי (*Ha-Ramai*)</note>.
